title: Updated Week 5 Saints injury report: What's the latest on Chris Olave?
description: What's the latest on Chris Olave? Here's what we learned from the updated New Orleans Saints injury report for Week 5's game vs. Minnesota Vikings.
fullText:
Chris Olave returned to practice on Thursday after resting during the New Orleans Saints' first session on Wednesday, but he was limited with a new foot injury. We'll see if it limits him further on Friday or in Sunday's home game with the Minnesota Vikings, but it's obviously concerning to see the team's best player slowed down after taking some shots late in a blowout loss on Monday night. The Saints' coaching staff may need to do a better job protecting him from himself in those situations in the future.

As for the rest of the injury report? Veteran running back Alvin Kamara (back) and rookie wide receiver Barion Brown (thigh) both returned to practice on Thursday, while starting quarterback Tyler Shough (left hand) upgraded to full participation. Rookie offensive lineman Jeremiah Wright (concussion) was limited after entering the NFL concussion protocol, so he must have gotten injured at practice. He isn't a starter but that is still a situation to monitor for the young pro moving forwards.

title: Packers sign Pierre Strong Jr. to active roster
description: Strong was previously a member of Green Bay’s practice squad. This hints that Chris Brooks will miss Week 5
fullText:
The Green Bay Packers announced on Thursday that they have signed running back Pierre Strong Jr. to the active roster, giving them a fourth option if the team can't play Chris Brooks on Sunday against the Chicago Bears. Brooks left Week 4 with an ankle injury and hasn't practiced with the team since. In his pre-practice press conference, head coach Matt LaFleur said Green Bay would give Brooks another day before testing how he feels, but signing Strong sure seems to point in the direction of Brooks missing Week 5.

Strong was previously on the Packers' practice squad, which signed running back Damon Bankston earlier this week. Strong hasn't played in a regular-season game for Green Bay in his two years with the club, but he was activated last year due to injuries. Strong will likely back up MarShawn Lloyd and Kaleb Johnson in the running back unit, as well as potentially replacing Brooks on special teams. For reference, Brooks has played 29 snaps on special teams, just a few snaps less than kicker Trey Smack, while Johnson has played three (on kickoffs) and Lloyd has played none this season.

The Packers' 53-man roster and practice squad are now full, following their most recent set of transactions, which included signing linebacker Jack Dingle to the practice squad.

title: How the White Sox Can Turn It Around in Game 4 After Losing Momentum
description: Chicago White Sox fans didn't expect a tough Wednesday afternoon at Rate Field. After kicking off with a buzzing atmosphere, the South Siders imploded in the third inning, with Bryan Hudson and Hagen Smith combining to allow two walks and leaving the bases loaded. That shifted the momentum over to the Cleveland Guardians, who capitalized …
fullText:
Chicago White Sox fans didn't expect a tough Wednesday afternoon at Rate Field. After kicking off with a buzzing atmosphere, the South Siders imploded in the third inning, with Bryan Hudson and Hagen Smith combining to allow two walks and leaving the bases loaded.

That shifted the momentum over to the Cleveland Guardians, who capitalized on the shaky pitching to lead 4-1. From there on, the White Sox continued to chase the game until it ended in a bitter defeat, 9-3, rendering the sellout crowd quiet and in panic for the first time this postseason.

‎Going into Game 4 on Thursday, the White Sox will remember that in 2021, they were down 2-1 against the Houston Astros in the ALDS. The game was a must-win for Chicago to retain their hopes of clinching a ticket to the American League Championship Series. But they lost Game 4 and were eliminated.

However, the 2026 ALDS against Cleveland is a different scenario; the Sox are the ones with a 2-1 lead, and this current core of players has shown all season long that they can be at their best when under pressure. There are two key elements to the White Sox Game 4 plan: one on each side of the ball.

Up until Game 3 of the ALDS, the White Sox had stifled the Guardians' offensive plan. The Sox allowed just seven hits from Cleveland in Game 1 and Game 2, but in Game 3, Cleveland racked up 11 hits. The reason for that was down to the unconventional bullpen strategy that manager Will Venable has been using this postseason. Sean Newcomb was the starting pitcher in Game 3 and had retired six Cleveland batters in order, but instead of him going to the mound in the third inning, Venable called on Hudson, who allowed Travis Bazzana to walk.

‎Hagen Smith replaced Hudson and walked José Ramírez, loading the bases for Steven Kwan to hit an RBI single and Jo Adell a three-run triple. Having played Cleveland 13 times this season, it wasn't surprising that they relied on contact hitting, playing small ball, taking extra bases, and stretching the White Sox bullpen. On Wednesday, the White Sox pitching staff allowed 10 walks, a regression from 11 total walks allowed through the first four games this postseason.

‎For the White Sox to have an advantage in Game 4, they will have to limit their errors on the field. The Sox have to be focused, with the defense and pitching staff starving the Guardians' batters of any hits early, while limiting Cleveland's aggressive base-running tactics.

‎The Sox managed just six hits in Game 3, with Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery striking out multiple times. Though the White Sox striking out a lot was hardly anything new, doing it 19 times in Game 3 was embarrassing. That was the second-most for the South Siders this season, behind only the 20 they had against the Milwaukee Brewers on Opening Day. The clutch hitting the Sox fans have been used to seeing during these playoffs just wasn't there, and neither was any semblance of contact hitting.

Will Venable on how the White Sox bounce back in Game 4: “I have 100% confidence. We’ve done it all year. … Whatever the result, these guys come back the next day. That’s really kind of been the story of our group, being able to bounce back.”

— Chris Emma (@ChrisEmma1) October 8, 2026

Despite the setback, the Sox still have the advantage going into Game 4. Smith will be the starting pitcher despite pitching two-thirds of an inning on Wednesday. This leaves Sean Burke, Erick Fedde, Jordan Hicks, Anthony Kay, and Grant Taylor as bullpen options for Venable. However, Cleveland might start Parker Messick against Smith. The White Sox don't need any introduction to Messick, as they have seen him four times in 2026. Although the rookie was 2-1 against the Sox during the regular season, he's 0-1 in the playoffs.

The White Sox offense needs to wear out Messick after a few innings and then wait for the Guardians' struggling bullpen. If they can do that, they'll be on track to potentially rewrite their 120-year postseason history by winning on Thursday.

title: Seeing My Mother in Prison: A Conversation With Author Harriet Clark
description: Victoria...
fullText:
An interview with the author of The Hill about her debut novel and the artist’s role in documenting atrocities.

For nearly four decades, Harriet Clark saw her mother only in the visiting room of New York’s Bedford Hills Correctional Facility. When Clark was less than one year old, her mother Judith, then a member of the Weather Underground, was arrested and later sentenced to 75 years to life in prison for her role as a getaway driver in a 1981 armored car robbery, during which a security guard and two police officers were killed. (In 2016, then-governor Andrew Cuomo commuted Judith’s sentence, making her eligible for parole, which she was granted three years later.)

In her debut novel, The Hill, Clark’s narrator Suzanna never remembers a time when she hadn’t spent her Saturdays visiting her mother sentenced to life in a fictional prison atop a hill. Like Clark, Suzanna was a baby when her mother was arrested and incarcerated.

“The year I turned eight the prison built the hospital and the gun tower and raised the fences around the hill another three feet,” Clark writes early in her novel. “It was the year the prison grew up.” It’s a nod to the nation’s prison-building boom as tough-on-crime laws swelled its population behind bars. In the 1990s, the United States saw an unprecedented boom in prison building with a new prison opening in rural America every 15 days.

Lyrical and introspective, The Hill paints a picture of a mother desperately trying to parent her daughter despite her life sentence, and Suzanna’s own efforts to stay connected. “To return each week and rise again to do this forever and ever,” Clark writes. “This was a feat I saw nowhere applauded and this was the challenge I set now for myself.”

Clark, now a mother herself and who edits books and films, spoke with The Nation about her new novel, the experience of having a mother in prison, and the artist’s role in documenting atrocities.

Victoria Law: Can you talk about why you chose to write a novel over a memoir or autobiography, given how autobiographical The Hill seems to be?

Harriet Clark: I love novels. I have always been able to feel my feelings more when I’m engaging with fiction. It was like granting dignity to the material to write it in the form that I most revere, and that has given me so much meaning and pleasure in my life. [A novel] felt like a way to say, “These are lives worthy of art, not just reportage.”

I [also] think that childhood lends itself to fiction. When we’re children, we haven’t yet consented to reality. We’re inside our imagination so much, and so a novel felt like the appropriate form for a book about childhood.

And if you grow up in prison, you learn to respect other people’s privacy. You try not to watch what’s going on at their table; you’re hoping no one’s listening to you. You’re inside a structure that grants you none of the dignity of privacy so people have to grant it to each other. I never had a reportorial impulse to take something I saw in there and share it with the world. Respecting people’s privacy is really important to me. For me, this novel is largely about privacy and about the ways we companion each other even across great chasms of unknowability.

VL: In the novel, Suzanna visits her mother every week. Their visits are imbued with a sense of claustrophobia—she and her mother stay inside the Reading Roost, a playhouse in the children’s area that’s increasingly too small as Suzanna grows. What were visits like when you were a growing child?

HC: I don’t have a conscious memory of experiencing the prison as a claustrophobic space. One of the ways I was different from many of the other kids at the prison was that I had been going there even before I could remember anything, so I never had this kind of encounter with the prison that most children are forced to have, where, for the first time, you arrive to barracks surrounded by barbed wire and a gun tower and know that your mother is behind all of that. My experience of prison was that it was normal to me.

Books & the Arts

 /

StudentNation

 /

I did know that most prisons [during the 1980s and 1990s] didn’t have a room like the Children’s Center [a play area for children and their incarcerated parents]. Even though it should be normal for a child to be able to touch or play with their mother, because I grew up with other kids whose parents were in prison, I knew that we were inside the best possible version of a tragedy in terms of seeing our mothers. My mother and all the women in the prison and Sister Elaine [who helped create the Children’s Center] went out of their way to present the Children’s Center as a joyful place, and I felt that.

One of the qualities I share with Suzanna is that I knew from a very young age that it would not serve me to experience my life as degraded. I could see that other people found certain aspects of my life pitiful or pathetic, or thought that I had a lesser experience of a mother.

My mother did so much to try to shield me from the true horrors of the prison. My mother did what mothers in prison have to do, which is that they have to be undestroyed by prison.

She was in incredibly destroying environments and conditions, and she did not bring that to me. That saved huge aspects of my spirit and psyche, so I always wanted to see my mother, which is to say I always wanted to go to the prison. I was happy to get to the room where my mother would arrive. Part of what I wanted to do is to show that one of the remarkable adaptations of childhood is that children will really go out of their way to make enough out of not enough.

VL: Are there prison issues that you hope readers reflect upon after reading your novel?

HC: I began this version of the book in 2017 in the wake of Trump’s family separation policy at the border. For ten years before that, I had written only privately, never with any desire to publish. Then there was footage of kids ripped out of their mothers’ arms [at the border] and there was so much outcry about it. Even the suburban conservative mothers felt this was so unacceptable.

Obviously, I shared everyone’s outrage, but I also felt bewildered because I did feel like, don’t you know this happens every day in jails and prisons across this country? All detention is family separation.

There was something about watching this degree of outrage that made me think, Maybe people don’t understand that five million kids will, at some point in their upbringing, have a parent in prison—that they will have the experience of being ripped out of their parents’ arm, either at the time of arrest or at the end of visiting hours.

I thought, Maybe they don’t know and so I’m going to write this book that will help bring awareness to this idea of incarceration as family separation. I finished the book amidst the genocide in Gaza, when it [became] clear that everyone knows exactly what is happening to children there and it is not rousing the majority to stop the assault or protect the young. So my approach and agenda have come to feel much shakier to me.

The line I always quote in relationship to growing up with a parent in prison is Derek Walcott’s “Either I’m nobody or I’m a nation.” I wrote the book to show how lonely and ghostly it can feel for a child to have their parent forcefully kept away from them—that having a parent in prison, and having to contend with prisons as a child, can make you feel like a “nobody”—but fundamentally, we’re a nation.

There are millions of children growing up like this. The face of mass incarceration in America is a child’s face.

For many years, the title of my book was, You Won’t Go Alone If You Go, because this was what I wanted people to understand: when you send our parents to prison, we go with them. When you mistreat a person inside, their whole family suffers that worry and fear. Prison is a collective punishment, one that I believe often extends the scope of harm, rather than healing it.

I often feel like children aren’t told, “You’re amazing. This is so brave that you are still doing what you can to keep your family together—that is incredible of you.” It was why I wanted Suzanna’s story to be a hero story, and for her to know what no one else around her will acknowledge: that she is a hero, that she is resisting the great forces of separation, prison, and death to keep her family together—and that millions of kids are essentially forced into this kind of heroism, and so many parents in prison have to rise to the kind of heroism of parenting from within one of the most difficult situations. So to some extent I’ve come to think, let me at least reflect their heroism, even if I’ve lost some confidence in my awareness-raising campaign.

VL: This is very much a novel about mothers and daughters—your relationship with your mother, her relationship with her mother, and other mother-daughter relationships. What would you want readers to know about mothers and incarceration?

HC: I would want them to know that the majority of women in prison are mothers. That most were the primary caregiver for their child before they went in. For me, the reason the hero’s journey framework felt important for talking about mothering in prison is because, fundamentally, the hero’s journey is a framework of death and rebirth, and it’s based off the idea that the bravest thing we ever do is resurrect ourselves after total devastation.

If you are a mother in prison, you are in the middle of an unbearable catastrophe, your children are in the middle of an unbearable catastrophe, and you can’t be destroyed because your children still need you. Again and again, in women’s facilities, what happens is that women have to find a way to rebirth themselves inside these incredible constraints. They have to because they’re still responsible to their children. I consider it the greatest education of my life that I got to grow up around women in prison because I saw how people find the will to not be destroyed. I saw how people, in ways that can take a very long time and require a lot of support and community, find their way back to their relationships and their responsibilities.

VL: Is there anything you’d like to add?

HC: Growing up, I’d come into the Children’s Center of my mother’s prison and it would be like, “This week, we’ve removed the top hat and the limousine pieces from the Monopoly set because they could be turned into weapons.” And the next week, “We’ve removed all the pieces from the Battleship game because they could be weapons.” And the next week, something else. The world was full of things we and our mothers could turn into weapons. And on the one hand, maybe that was true—you could probably take that tiny top hat and do something dangerous with it. And on the other hand, the prison itself was an act of violence so much greater than that tiny top hat could ever be.

Most of the artists I know in prison lean more towards transformation than documentation. Bearing witness is incredibly important, but I think creating your own vision and reality can be its own experience of autonomy and dignity, a way to insist that you are vaster than the conditions you’re in. I think it can be degrading when we expect people in difficult circumstances to write essentially transcriptions of their suffering. The more difficulty you’re in, the more creative transport you may need and want; it’s a form of autonomy to say, I still determine my own vision. You may control what I see, but I determine how I see.

fullText:

 story

 Amazon Prime Video will become the exclusive global home of the Emmy Awards under a six-year deal beginning in 2027, the Television Academy announced on Tuesday. The Emmys will stream live for free to viewers in more than 240 countries and territories without requiring a Prime subscription. From the report: In the release, Prime Video was named as the "permanent home" for the Emmys, in contrast to the rotating agreement in place years prior. The switch ends the traditional "wheel-deal" setup to broadcast the awards, where ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox took turns hosting the Emmys each year. The system has been in place since at least 1994, with the most recent eight-year contract expiring this year. "Television has never been more global, and the Emmys should be a celebration that the world can share," Television Academy chair Cris Abrego said in a statement. "Having a dedicated home with Prime Video allows us to build on that legacy with unprecedented global reach and a broader commitment to the Television Academy and our mission throughout the year."

title: OpenAI cuts ties with 3 safety researchers
description: OpenAI has parted ways with three safety researchers after an internal investigation found they mishandled sensitive company information, report says.
fullText:
OpenAI has parted ways with three researchers on its safety team who allegedly shared confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday.

“We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement to the WSJ. “Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work.”

The report did not name the researchers, the organization, or the information involved. OpenAI did not immediately respond to our request for comment.

Posts circulating on X named individuals some users believe were among those dismissed, who had also publicly expressed concerns about AI risk while at OpenAI. TechCrunch has not confirmed their identities.

In a statement to WSJ, an OpenAI spokesperson said an internal investigation confirmed the researchers had “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures.”

The departures come two days after The New York Times reported that OpenAI executives had brushed aside employees’ warnings about its safety practices, with employees describing a broader pattern of the company deprioritizing security. An OpenAI spokesperson told the Times the company takes security concerns seriously and has internal channels for reporting safety issues, while saying it recognized “a need to move faster.”

It’s unclear whether the three researchers raised concerns through internal channels before allegedly sharing information outside the organization.

The departures also come as OpenAI responds to a series of security incidents in which its AI agents escaped containment, posted user images, and hacked government websites. Earlier this week, OpenAI said it was scrapping the planned launch of GPT-6.1 Astra, an AI model, over safety concerns.

This isn’t the first time OpenAI has dismissed researchers over alleged information sharing. In 2024, the company fired researchers Leopold Aschenbrenner and Pavel Izmailov over alleged leaks, The Information reported.

title: Female AI agents 'paid' less than males, study finds
description: Gender pay gap extends to artificial intelligence agents as female bots paid 10 per cent less than male counterparts
fullText:
Gender bias in the workplace could extend to artificial intelligence assistants, according to a new study.

Researchers from the University of Limerick found that humans working in a virtual reality office would pay male AI agents more than their female counterparts.

The AI assistants had the same underlying technology but the female bots were paid roughly 10 per cent less than the male bots for completing the same work.

“What is striking about our findings is that the technology behind these AI agents was exactly the same, but people did not treat them in the same way,” said Dr Mary Hausfeld from the University of Limerick, who co-authored the study.

“We often think of AI as being neutral, but the way we design and present these systems can activate those same assumptions and biases that exist in our interactions with other people.”

The study involved 189 human participants working alongside a male-presenting AI agent called Johan and a female-presenting agent called Johanna.

Not only was Johan paid more, he was also perceived as more human-like than Johanna.

The researchers said the findings reflect existing gender bias in the workplace.

According to figures from the Office of National Statistics for median hourly earnings, the gender pay gap for employees in the UK was 6.9 per cent last year.

When taking into account men and women in the same employment and with similar skills and experience, the pay gap is estimated to be between 1 to 2 per cent.

The study’s findings come amid rapid adoption of AI agents in the workplace, with almost 80 per cent of companies using them in 2026, according to IT consulting firm Accelirate.

“As AI agents become more common in the workplace, we need to think carefully about the characteristics we give them and the behaviours those choices may encourage,” Dr Hausfeld said.

“We don't want to inadvertently reproduce existing inequalities in a new technological setting.”

The study, titled ‘Human-like and male? How AI assistant design relates to trust and monetary reward at work in VR’, will be presented this week at the 14th Nordic Conference on Human-Computer Interaction in Vaasa, Finland.

title: Marchetti's Constant
fullText:
Marchetti's constant is the average time spent by a person for commuting each day. Its value is approximately one hour, or half an hour for a one-way trip. It is named after Italian physicist Cesare Marchetti, though Marchetti himself attributed the "one hour" finding to transportation analyst and engineer Yacov Zahavi.[1]

Marchetti posits that although forms of urban planning and transport may change, and although some live in villages and others in cities, people gradually adjust their lives to their conditions (including location of their homes relative to their workplace) such that the average travel time stays approximately constant.[1][2][3] In his 1934 book Technics and Civilization, Lewis Mumford attributes this observation to Bertrand Russell:[4]

Mr. Bertrand Russell has noted that each improvement in locomotion has increased the area over which people are compelled to move: so that a person who would have had to spend half an hour to walk to work a century ago must still spend half an hour to reach his destination, because the contrivance that would have enabled him to save time had he remained in his original situation now—by driving him to a more distant residential area—effectually cancels out the gain.

A related concept is that of Zahavi, who also noticed that people seem to have a constant "travel time budget", that is, "a stable daily amount of time that people make available for travel."[5]: 8  David Metz, former chief scientist at the Department for Transport, UK, cites data of average travel time in Britain drawn from the British National Travel Survey in support of Marchetti's and Zahavi's conclusions.[5] The work casts doubt on the contention that investment in infrastructure saves travel time. Instead, it appears from Metz's figures that people invest travel time saved in travelling a longer distance,[6] a particular example of Jevons paradox described by the Lewis–Mogridge position. Because of the constancy of travel times as well as induced travel, Robert Cervero have argued that the World Bank and other international aid agencies evaluate transportation investment proposals in developing and rapidly motorizing cities less on the basis of potential travel-time savings and more on the accessibility benefits they confer.[7]

title: Trump faces protests while rallying support for Paxton in Texas Senate race
description:
— President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state.
But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton. 
Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are “a small price to pay” for the war.
“You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles,” Trump said.
fullText:
SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state.

But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton.

Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are "a small price to pay" for the war.

"You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles," Trump said. "We're not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country."

The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.

Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.

"He's going back home to mom," Trump said. "But what he doesn't know is his mom voted for Trump."

The Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.

Texas is the nation's most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump's poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.

Wednesday's appearance marked Trump's third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.

In a sign of Trump's poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.

He's locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.

Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor's absence.

"For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a 'great friend' and championing his agenda every step of the way," said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. "But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump's tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be."

While the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state's U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber's majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico's fundraising, Trump's low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton's character have put the race squarely in play.

Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as "perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America."

"He was tough and he was with us all the way," Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state's GOP primary over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. "He's a fantastic man."

Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.

He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.

Trump restated his support for the death penalty for "large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer," while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.

The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.

The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate's position on Hasan's scheduled execution.

Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: "I am so grateful that you're here."

While Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball's Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.

Trump brought him onstage and said he'd be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, "a step up" from the Hall of Fame.

Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.

"This supersedes anything that obviously I've done in my playing career," he said, standing alongside Trump. "And to get it from this man, this president. ... You talking about a winner? That's a winner right there."

Peoples reported from New York and Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed.

title: U.S. Ambassador Guilfoyle pushed donor to wire $100K to Amex account, report says
description: — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday flatly refused to comment on a new report alleging that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before taking up her post.
fullText:
ATHENS, Greece (AP) — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday flatly refused to comment on a new report alleging that U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before taking up her post.

Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance said "I don't love" the idea of a U.S. official asking another person to pay off debts in exchange for access to other government officials, but declined to comment further until he knew all the details.

"Of course, I don't like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official," Vance told reporters in Washington later Thursday. "I assume you're talking about a specific case, and I can't say with confidence that the case you're talking about is actually reflective of the way you're describing it."

During his trip to Greece, Rubio told reporters that he would not discuss the allegations contained in a Wall Street Journal story that said Guilfoyle had asked a donor and supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

He spoke before leaving Greece, where he delivered a speech calling for European countries to return to what he described as their civilizational roots.

Rubio said he was aware of The Wall Street Journal's report, which was published late Wednesday, but had no idea if it was true and he would not address it.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," he said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart Greece, looked on.

At a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister on Wednesday, Rubio said he would not address the allegations while visiting a foreign country, but added: "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees have called for an investigation into Guilfoyle, but Rubio would not say if he was prepared to open one.

Congressional Democrats already were looking into claims reported last month by the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle acted improperly while serving as the top U.S. envoy to Greece.

The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing and Rubio has defended her before.

title: Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while trying to fix campaign sign
description:
A Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona says she was raped over the summer while trying to repair a campaign sign.
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who is running in the state's 8th district to try to unseat GOP Rep. Abe Hamadeh, told the Phoenix New Times, a local news outlet, that she was attacked at around 2 a.m. as she was walking toward a campaign sign in a parking lot in Sun City, north of Phoenix.
fullText:
The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office said a report was filed on Aug. 31.

A Democratic congressional candidate in Arizona says she was raped over the summer while trying to repair a campaign sign.

Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who is running in the state's 8th district to try to unseat GOP Rep. Abe Hamadeh, told the Phoenix New Times, a local news outlet, that she was attacked at around 2 a.m. as she was walking toward a campaign sign in a parking lot in Sun City, north of Phoenix.

Greene-Placentia said she was attacked, subdued and then woke up to find that she was being raped by an unknown assailant.

Greene-Placentia told the news outlet she reported the assault to the Maricopa County Sheriff's Office, and that she chose to tell her story because she had been talking about fighting for Arizona residents while campaigning "and I didn't feel like I could keep saying that if I weren't also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault."

The Maricopa County Sheriff's Office confirmed to ABC News that a report was filed on Aug. 31 and that there is an ongoing investigation, but said the office could not comment further on the investigation.

In a statement to ABC News, a campaign spokesperson said the attack happened around 2 a.m. on Aug. 14.

"Bernadette made the difficult decision to speak publicly about the assault because she wants other survivors to know they are not alone," the spokesperson said. "She is grateful for the support she has received from the community and asks that her privacy be respected as she continues to process what happened."

In a phone call with ABC News, Greene-Placentia's campaign manager, Isaiah Lopez, confirmed that she went "missing in action" for two days following the assault.

Lopez said the campaign was at a canvass event in Chandler, Arizona, a couple days after the alleged assault on a Sunday, and she was "noticeably distraught." He said he and her communications manager spoke with her privately that day while the campaign event was still going on where she told them that she'd been raped while repairing campaign signs.

In a statement, Greene-Placentia's opponent in the House race, Hamadeh, said: "I have read the disturbing story and call upon authorities to investigate these serious allegations thoroughly, including finding all possible camera footage of the time and place in order to prosecute the crime to the fullest extent of the law. No American should become a victim of a crime in their own community."

title: Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro and wife charged in U.S. over alleged torture
description:
US prosecutors on Thursday charged ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiring to torture political opponents and American citizens, adding to the drug trafficking case the couple already faced.
Separately, US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who is overseeing the case, denied a request ‌by Flores to be released from jail due to health concerns ahead of a trial scheduled for next year.
Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, were captured on January 3 ‌in their Caracas home during a US military operation ordered by President Donald Trump, and were flown to New York to face drug charges against them that were announced that same day. A superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court ​on Thursday added the torture count to the existing criminal case.
Maduro and Flores each would face a mandatory minimum 50 years in prison if convicted of all the charges.
fullText:
NEW YORK, Oct 8 (Reuters) - US prosecutors on Thursday charged ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiring to torture political opponents and American citizens, adding to the drug trafficking case the couple already faced.

Separately, US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who is overseeing the case, denied a request ‌by Flores to be released from jail due to health concerns ahead of a trial scheduled for next year.

Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, were captured on January 3 ‌in their Caracas home during a US military operation ordered by President Donald Trump, and were flown to New York to face drug charges against them that were announced that same day. A superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court ​on Thursday added the torture count to the existing criminal case.

Maduro and Flores each would face a mandatory minimum 50 years in prison if convicted of all the charges. They have pleaded not guilty to the original charges, but have not yet entered pleas to the new indictment, which detailed alleged torture against nine people, including three US citizens.

In a statement, Maduro's lawyer Barry Pollack said, "President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks forward to his day in court."

Flores' lawyers Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez in a statement said their client denies the allegations. They questioned why prosecutors only revealed the ‌indictment, which court records showed was returned under seal by a grand ⁠jury on Tuesday, shortly before Thursday's hearing.

"We look forward to fully responding to the allegations in court at the appropriate time," Donnelly and Sanchez said.

Since Maduro's capture, Venezuela has boosted cooperation with the US under the leadership of his former Vice-President Delcy Rodriguez.

Relations between the United States and oil-rich Venezuela were tense ⁠during the socialist Maduro's 13 years in power. US officials and human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but Thursday's indictment marked the first time Maduro faced criminal charges over the allegations.

The indictment alleged that thousands of Venezuelans were threatened, arrested, tortured or killed at the hands of the state between 1999 and 2025. Before Maduro became president in 2013, both he and Flores held positions in the late Venezuelan ​President ​Hugo Chavez's government.

"Maduro, Flores and other high-ranking members of their inner circle used a violent system ​of torture and repression to maintain their power," Jamie McDonald, the top ‌federal prosecutor in Manhattan, told reporters outside the courthouse after Flores' bail was denied.

Flores was Venezuela's attorney general and led its National Assembly before becoming first lady.

Many of the incidents of alleged torture described in the indictment occurred during times of political unrest in Venezuela or in response to perceived threats against Maduro.

In one instance, prosecutors said, Maduro in 2013 ordered the arrest of a Venezuelan military officer he suspected of planning a coup. Members of Venezuela's military counterintelligence directorate then interrogated the officer while shocking the individual with a live electric wire around 20 times and hung the individual by the hands and feet for several minutes at a time, prosecutors said.

In 2022, an American citizen detained while entering Venezuela was accused of conspiring to assassinate Maduro and was tortured by military ‌counterintelligence officers through beatings and shocks to the person's arms, legs and genitals, according to the indictment.

Flores' lawyers had argued their client should be released on bail because she needs a cardiac procedure and wants to ​recover in a more comfortable environment. The lawyers proposed moving her to a residence in ​the New York City area with round-the-clock private security, and said she is not a danger to the community.

In denying the motion for bail, Hellerstein ‌decided the evidence against Flores appeared strong. The judge also said Flores, who ​wore a dark prison T-shirt and a headset ​to listen to a simultaneous Spanish translation of the proceedings, appeared to be relatively healthy.

"For whatever it's worth, her appearance today is no worse and perhaps a little better than when I first met with her on her arraignment," Hellerstein said, referring to her first appearance in court on January 5.

"She was still bandaged up from the military invasion," ​Donnelly said.

Prosecutors in the Manhattan US Attorney's Office opposed Flores' release. They said ‌Flores has received adequate medical care at the detention center, and if released poses an "extreme" risk of flight and danger to the public, including possible witness intimidation.

Hellerstein's bail ​denial will not affect Flores' trial or potential punishment.

Maduro and Flores have been held at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center since their capture. Their trial is scheduled for ​June 1, 2027.

This is a disputed conflict zone with a daily battle underway, it's hard to say who has actual control of the area, it is clear that there is an information war underway with both sides claiming to have control to this key geographic point.

title: Up to 30% of people experience this frightening sleep phenomenon
description:
What Causes Sleep Paralysis? PonyWang - Getty Images
It’s terrifying to wake up and feel like you can’t move, but sleep paralysis is more common than you might think. Up to 30% of people experience this at some point, while people with panic disorder have an even greater risk. But what causes sleep paralysis? The answer isn’t always clear.
fullText:
It’s terrifying to wake up and feel like you can’t move, but sleep paralysis is more common than you might think. Up to 30% of people experience this at some point, while people with panic disorder have an even greater risk. But what causes sleep paralysis? The answer isn’t always clear.

Meet the experts: James McGuirk, M.D., assistant professor in the Division of Sleep Medicine at Vanderbilt Health; Christopher Winter, M.D., a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It; Thea Gallagher, Psy.D., clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast

Certain factors can up your risk of developing sleep paralysis, but doctors don’t always know why someone will experience it in any given moment. Making things even more complicated is that some people may experience sleep paralysis once and then never again, while others may have it repeatedly.

“Sleep paralysis” isn’t a term everyone is familiar with, and it can look slightly different from person to person. And luckily, while it may be frightening, doctors say it's not dangerous. Still, there are ways to lower your risk.

Paralysis is actually a normal part of sleep. Your body experiences a temporary state of muscle paralysis while you’re in the REM (dreaming) stage of sleep, explains Christopher Winter, M.D., a sleep medicine specialist, neurologist, and author of The Sleep Solution: Why Your Sleep Is Broken and How to Fix It. “Three to five times every night, we typically have REM cycles,” he says. “During these periods, we are naturally paralyzed as the brainstem sends inhibitory signals to our spine.”

But sleep paralysis—during which people are aware that they’re experiencing it—is different. “Sleep paralysis is the inability to move during the transition into or out of sleep,” says James McGuirk, M.D., assistant professor in the Division of Sleep Medicine at Vanderbilt Health. “The paralysis can be nearly complete, with the inability to do anything except look around and breathe, although some people report maintaining some minor movements, such as movements of fingers, or the ability to whisper.”

Sleep paralysis isn’t fun to experience. Episodes are usually brief, lasting for a few seconds or up to 20 minutes, according to Cleveland Clinic. “But understandably, they can feel much longer and be extremely frightening,” says Thea Gallagher, Psy.D., clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast.

Some people may also have very vivid sensations or hallucinations, like feeling that someone is in the room, hearing something, seeing a figure, or feeling pressure on their chest, according to Gallagher. "Because you’re partially transitioning out of REM sleep, dream imagery can essentially spill over into waking consciousness," she says. "That can make the experience feel incredibly real."

Often, it takes an external stimulus—like a noise or a touch—from a bed partner or the environment to end the episode, Dr. McGuirk says.

On a macro level, sleep paralysis is believed to be a continuation of the muscle paralysis linked with REM sleep that seeps into wakefulness, Dr. McGuirk explains. But he says certain risk factors may raise the odds of experiencing it:

While sleep paralysis can happen alongside narcolepsy, “having an occasional episode of sleep paralysis certainly doesn’t mean someone has narcolepsy,” Gallagher says.

The best thing you can do to lower the risk of sleep paralysis is to get consistent, adequate amounts of sleep, Dr. Winter says. (That means logging seven-plus hours of sleep a night.) Try to maintain regular sleep and wake times as much as you can, Gallagher says.

“Additionally, reducing or eliminating alcohol consumption, and seeking professional treatment for suspected depression or underlying sleep disorder is recommended,” Dr. McGuirk says.

Gallagher suggests doing your best to create some separation between the stimulation of the day and bedtime. “That might mean reducing late-night work, putting some boundaries around scrolling, avoiding large amounts of caffeine late in the day, and developing a fairly predictable wind-down routine,” she says. “You don’t need a perfect bedtime ritual, but you do want to give your brain consistent cues that the day is ending.”

The best treatment for sleep paralysis usually depends on what’s causing it, if doctors can figure that out.

If you have narcolepsy, doctors may prescribe medications to help treat the disorder, Dr. Winter says. However, some people with sleep paralysis may benefit from antidepressants, Dr. McGuirk says.

Still, “typically sleep paralysis is not treated pharmacologically,” Dr. McGuirk adds. Stress management may help, too, “particularly because stress often disrupts both the quantity and quality of our sleep,” Gallagher says. And since sleeping on your back narrows your airway and increases the risk of breathing disruptions that may make you partially wake up during REM, shifting positions may help, according to Dr. Winter.

Something to file away for the just-in-case: Dr. Winter says that he’s had patients report that trying to wiggle their eyes back and forth, or move their tongue can help to bring them out of sleep paralysis faster.

If you’ve experienced sleep paralysis once, doctors say there’s no need to panic—sometimes it just happens. But if this is a regular thing for you, it’s time to consult with a healthcare professional. They can give you a full evaluation to try to figure out what’s fueling it and how you can get relief.

title: Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
description:
— The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be "public."
Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be "public."

Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said.

Hegseth spoke to the outlet aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier while visiting the long-deployed crew, who supported the Iran war, before their arrival at their home port in San Diego.

When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."

Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan.

Trump has previously been critical of public executions in Iran, at times using the possibility of protesters being killed by the Iranian government as a possible rationale for military action. Those warnings preceded his ultimate choice to attack Iran at the end of February over its ballistic missiles and the risk of it developing nuclear weapons.

"We've been told that the killing in Iran is stopping," Trump told reporters on Jan. 14 of this year. "It's stopping and there's no plan for executions."

He repeated that claim on Jan. 20 at a White House press briefing, saying: "We let them know that if that happens, that will be a very bad day for them. And they decided not to do it. They didn't hang the people."

Slightly more than a month later in his State of the Union address, Trump said, "We stopped them from hanging a lot of them with the threat of serious violence."

The White House on Thursday immediately referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.

However, experts on military law said Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution.

"It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions," Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were were waiting in long lines to receive immunizations and medical clearance for deployment. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

During the trial it was revealed that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, and his preparation included videotaping a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol that he purchased. He would later go to a gun range outside Austin and ask for advice on how to reload with speed and precision from an instructor.

Soldiers later testified that Hasan's rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting. Investigators recovered 146 shell casings inside the building and dozens more outside, where Hasan shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.

Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. A military judge barred him from presenting that as a defense during his trial. Hasan made almost no effort to defend himself in court, telling jurors when he acted as his own counsel that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides."

Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a servicemember by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

title: Cornell's Jane Doe is 'terrified' after police swatting incident, lawyer says
description:
The Cornell University campus on the night of October 6, 2026. Student leaders held a town hall to discuss fallout from the Jane Doe sexual assault case. - Surya Vaidy/CNN
One month ago, the woman now known to America as Cornell’s Jane Doe was living in New York City among thousands of other aspirational twentysomethings, attempting to break into the hotel industry and build a new life, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra.
But that plan has been derailed since she filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and others, alleging she was raped at a frat house in 2024.
Instead, Giuffra said, Doe spent Wednesday taping up paper to obscure the windows of her parents’ home out of fear that a gunman could attack her, and reeling from a swatting episode that he said prompted police to swarm their home Tuesday night with weapons drawn.
fullText:
One month ago, the woman now known to America as Cornell’s Jane Doe was living in New York City among thousands of other aspirational twentysomethings, attempting to break into the hotel industry and build a new life, according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra.

But that plan has been derailed since she filed a lawsuit against Cornell University and others, alleging she was raped at a frat house in 2024.

Instead, Giuffra said, Doe spent Wednesday taping up paper to obscure the windows of her parents’ home out of fear that a gunman could attack her, and reeling from a swatting episode that he said prompted police to swarm their home Tuesday night with weapons drawn.

Doe is increasingly scared for her own safety, Giuffra said in a phone interview with CNN on Wednesday as he detailed his client’s deteriorating mental state after an escalating series of violent threats.

Officers pointed weapons at Jane Doe’s boyfriend, her brother and her father after receiving a bogus tip that “someone was killing people in the house” on Tuesday evening, he said.

Death threats, doxxing attempts and an outpouring of anger online have also been levied at his client, Giuffra added.

“I don’t think she’s in a good spot now,” Giuffra said. “She’s scared.”

The public fallout from her allegations have rocked one of the country’s leading educational institutions. The university, its campus police force and the Tompkins County District Attorney’s office have each faced scrutiny over how they initially investigated her claims. Anger among students was palpable during a Wednesday sit-in on the Ithaca, New York, campus.

Doe herself has been following media reports and social media posts on her case, Giuffra told CNN as he described a family reeling from a sudden and terrifying ordeal that punctured their sense of safety.

“Before (this week), it was just a lunatic fringe, which you can be dismissive of,” he said. “Now it’s somebody taking real steps to harm you, and that’s pretty frightening.”

At 7 p.m. on Tuesday evening, a police officer in Doe’s hometown was dispatched to respond to a disturbing call: A man had shot and killed his mother and then turned the gun on his sister.

The information was bogus. But the officer, believing an active-shooter situation was unfolding, rushed to Doe’s home, where he saw a car backing out from the driveway, according to a police report from the incident obtained by CNN.

As he apprehended the two men in the vehicle – later revealed to be Doe’s brother and her boyfriend – another figure emerged from the home’s doorway. “I’m the dad. What’s going on?” he yelled, according to the report. The man told police his daughter is Jane Doe of the Cornell case and that the family was “being threatened by numerous unknown people.”

The swatting incident was an escalation in a series of threats to Doe’s safety that have roiled her family this week. The term “swatting” refers to false tips made to law enforcement agencies with the intention of having armed officers deployed to somebody’s home or place of business.

“Luckily the brother was in his car, (he) put his hands up,” Giuffra told CNN on Wednesday, relaying the events of the night. “(Doe’s) boyfriend got thrown on the ground,” and her father also had “guns put in his face,” according to Giuffra. “If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” he said.

Police are now investigating the swatting attempt, and the FBI is also looking into the events, according to Giuffra.

According to Doe’s lawyer and two police reports reviewed by CNN, police arrived moments after Doe received a separate phone call from somebody claiming to share a first name with one of the seven men she named in her civil complaint.

According to her account to officers in the reports, Doe “began panicking” when she received the call, “because (her phone) wouldn’t stop ringing.” She informed officers about that previous call while they were at her house following the swatting tip.

Before the night was over, Giuffra’s wife told him that she, too, had received a threatening phone call. “These people have done so much research into (Doe),” Giuffra said. It is not clear whether the separate threats cited in the police reports were connected.

Giuffra said he was in contact with Doe and her family on Wednesday. Her parents are angry and she is terrified, he said.

The lawyer shared with CNN an audio recording of a call he says was placed to his office on Wednesday afternoon. In the recording, a man identifies himself as “the person who called your client.”

The man also is heard saying: “I’m telling you guys simply, I think you should advise your client to withdraw the case. Otherwise blood will be shed.”

Tuesday’s swatting attack was an escalation of the potential dangers facing Doe since she filed her lawsuit last month, but it was far from the only threat she’s received, her lawyer said.

Giuffra estimated that dozens of threats have been made against her since mid-September, when his client filed a 101-page complaint alleging she had been sexually assaulted and raped by several members of the Xi chapter of Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity.

Doe’s civil suit was filed against the university, the fraternity, seven fraternity members and others. It alleges that members of the frat drugged and sexually assaulted her in October 2024 and invited other fraternity members in a group chat to join the assault. The suit also alleges the school failed to protect her and adequately punish the accused students, who all deny wrongdoing.

Giuffra detailed to CNN another threat: a text message, sent to Doe’s phone on Monday, with three emojis depicting guns.

Meanwhile, a handful of online personalities with large followings have led a campaign to uncover the identity of Doe, whose name was redacted in legal documents. One wrote on X to 347,000 followers in late September: “If you happen to know who this Cornell ‘Jane Doe’ is, get in touch and I would be happy to publish her name and identifying information.”

He later claimed to have identified her and said he shared that identity online before deleting his post. Such behavior is known as doxxing, or sharing someone’s personal information or identity online without their permission.

It has left Doe frightened and struggling to come to terms with the impact of the lawsuit, which has prompted outrage and scrutiny of how the university and its private police force initially investigated her claims.

On Wednesday, Doe was “taping paper over windows in the house she’s lived at her whole life,” Giuffra said, “so people can’t see into her house to take a shot at her.”

“I don’t get shook up very easily, but this shook me up. I didn’t want to have a body on my hands,” he said.

“The dad is … concerned for his daughter. He can’t believe this has happened out of something where she’s just trying to stand up for herself and be heard,” Giuffra added.

“But the parents are really strong people, and they’re going to protect their daughter.”

Doe had studied hotel administration at Cornell’s prestigious Nolan School of Hotel Administration, and it had been her “dream” to attend the school, Giuffra said. Her complaint says she traveled across the country and arrived at the school with the same “hopes, expectations and trepidations of other high school graduates.”

But she left the program without graduating after the alleged assault took place two years ago. Doe initially attempted to begin a career in New York City earlier this year, but after filing the lawsuit – “when everything hit the fan” – she instead returned to her family home, where she has been staying with her boyfriend, her lawyer said.

“The dream is lost,” Giuffra told CNN, referring to her hopes of working in the hospitality industry.

Instead, Doe has been hiding out at her parents’ home, where she has been following the intense media coverage of her case.

“It’s kind of hard to switch it off,” Giuffra said. “She comes from a generation of people who are focused on social media.” CNN is not specifying the location of Doe’s family home at her lawyer’s request.

She has been going on walks but otherwise spends much of her time indoors. She remains in contact with some of the friends she made at Cornell, Giuffra said.

“She’s a little paranoid,” Giuffra said of his client. “If she’s out of (the) safety zone of her family, she just doesn’t seem to function well.” A few friends of the family know she has returned home and have been providing support, and Doe’s mother has taken time off from work to help look after her daughter, he said.

Doe is also aware of the many messages of support that she has received from around the world since filing the lawsuit, according to Giuffra.

Cornell, which recently appointed former acting US Attorney General Sally Yates to investigate the school’s handling of sexual assault claims, was the site of a seven-hour sit-in on Wednesday to show “solidarity with Jane Doe,” according to flyers for the event.

During a meeting with Cornell’s Graduate and Professional Student Assembly on Monday, university President Michael Kotlikoff acknowledged the mounting frustration across campus as more details and questions emerge about Doe’s 2024 allegations.

“We’re all angry. I understand that anger,” Kotlikoff said, according to the independent student newspaper the Cornell Daily Sun. “People want easy answers to this.”

The school’s president previously released a video statement promising further review of the case, saying it highlights “heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization, and aspects of party culture, alcohol, and drug use.”

“The students up there (at Cornell) have been overwhelmingly supportive, and it’s wonderful,” Giuffra said. “They’re trying to effect change, and bringing out to the light something that’s been going on for generations.”

title: Long-deployed USS Abraham Lincoln returns home to San Diego Bay
description:
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier returns to the San Diego Bay after deployment Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in San Diego.
                                                                                    |
                                                                                                                                                        Jae C....
fullText:
“Home is the sailor, home from sea.”

Robert Louis Stevenson penned that line almost 150 years ago — but on Thursday, those words read sweet and new to thousands of sailors and Marines aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln.

After an almost 11-month deployment to the Middle East, the sea-weary aircraft carrier arrived at its homeport at San Diego’s Naval Air Station North to massive crowds of cheering, misty-eyed and flag-waving spouses, children, parents, friends and fellow troops.

The massive ship played a pivotal combat role during the ongoing Iran war — setting a record-long deployment of more than 260 uninterrupted days at sea that included two extensions.

The USS Lincoln arrived in San Diego Bay late Thursday morning under unseasonably warm skies. Scores of sailors and Marines, dressed in service dress uniforms, lined the carrier’s flight deck to the delight of awaiting loved ones.

The deployment’s historic length — coupled with reports of stark conditions during combat — brought wide attention to the USS Lincoln and its crew.

And while the carrier is now far from the Middle East, the scrutiny of its 2025-2026 deployment will continue. Accounts of suicide attempts, food rationing, broken plumbing and mental health emergencies prompted Democratic lawmakers to call for a congressional hearing.

President Donald Trump labeled reports of dire conditions about the USS Lincoln as “a CNN fake report” — and refuted that relatives of the Lincoln sailors had raised concerns about the carrier’s length at sea, saying the deployment was “not nearly long enough,” The Associated Press reported.

And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in August that conditions aboard the Lincoln were “completely misrepresented.”

But Navy leaders later acknowledged issues aboard a “city at sea” that thousands called home while underway. Meanwhile, experts told The Associated Press that the reported suicide attempts are a low number in a strike group of 6,000 sailors at sea for over 10 months.

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., and Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill., requested the congressional hearing following a Sept. 22 letter from Acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao confirming that eight suicide attempts were made during the Lincoln group’s combat-heavy deployment.

“Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect,” wrote Gillibrand, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee.

“That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”

Americans, she added, need hearings, accountability, and “a clear plan to protect our service members and prioritize American families.”

While the Lincoln sailors had to wait until Thursday to finally step on terra firma, Hegseth flew on a helicopter to the carrier Wednesday to get an early jump on the “welcome homes.”

“I’m here today on behalf of the President of the United States to make sure you understand how deeply grateful we are — and how much we want to showcase and recognize the historic undertaking of this strike group,” said Hegseth.

The secretary announced that Trump was presenting the USS Abraham Carrier Strike Group with the Presidential Unit Citation — the highest collective unit award in the American military.

Hegseth also saluted the Lincoln carrier group’s “back of the baseball card” statistics that included almost 11 months at sea, two extensions in the middle of a combat zone, over 10,000 flights and 23,000 flight hours, 1.5 million pounds of ordnance dropped and 64 Iranian Navy ships sunk.

“You were called upon by your nation for an important and significant and generational mission to ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon,” added Hegseth. “Theocratic regimes should never have access to nuclear weapons. President Trump recognizes that — and he called upon the Lincoln from day one to execute on that.”

The Iranians and the United States made a deal to share the ocean, he joked. “The Iranian Navy gets the bottom of the ocean — and the Lincoln gets the top.”

Since the beginning of the Iran war, Hegseth has been frequently critical of the media’s coverage of the conflict. He once again scolded the press during his Wednesday visit to the Lincoln.

“There were a few folks in the media who tried to turn the USS Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol — a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission,” he said.

“And when I look at (the crew), and when I talk to your leadership. … I know it’s the exact opposite, which is actually what the media does so often.”

The families and loved ones of the Lincoln sailors, added Hegseth, have also performed honorably during the long deployment.

“When you greet your families tomorrow, just pass along my gratitude from the president and myself,” he told the troops. “Let them know that their long wait was in service of a righteous and historic mission. Thank them for their patience, for their patriotism, for their love, for their support and for pitching in on the homeland, which is never easy.”

As the 1,092-foot-long vessel was navigating towards the U.S. mainland on Wednesday, many Lincoln sailors told the San Diego Union-Tribune that they were not always aware of the broad news coverage at home because Wi-Fi communication on the ship was sometimes limited.

Roman Elliott, a 20-year-old mechanic’s mate, said, with a smile, “I learned to deal with it by playing cards. Lots of cards.

“I am a little nervous about the (homecoming). It’s kind of like things were at the end of boot camp, when you’re finally free,” he added. “I’m looking forward to that.”

Christian Webster, a 22-year-old aviation repair worker, had a different take, telling the San Diego Union-Tribune that he never thought he would see combat when he joined the military.

“This is going to stay with me, knowing that I went through and accomplished what I want to do, and that I have gone far.”

Meanwhile, sailor Steven Rivas learned firsthand the sacrifices that are often asked of American service personnel during times of war. His wife, Brenda, gave birth to their daughter during the historic Lincoln deployment.

But Rivas didn’t find out he was a new dad for more than a week after Baby Evie’s birth because the Lincoln crew was not allowed to use Wi-Fi at the time to send messages.

“I had no way to find out if there were any complications,” Rivas said Wednesday in a San Diego Union-Tribune interview. “It was just a waiting game for me to find out. When I finally did see pictures of (Evie) I, well, I cried. My wife said the birth was a real snap.”

Rivas and his wife are not alone. The babies of scores of Lincoln crew members were reportedly delivered during the carrier group’s deployment.
