title: Evans to defend title in extended WRC calendar including Scotland
description: The inaugural Rally Scotland will take place in October as the 2027 World Rally Championship comes to the BBC.
fullText:
The inaugural Rally Scotland will take place from 3-7 October in an extended 2027 World Rally Championship (WRC) calendar released by the FIA and the sport's promoters.

The gravel event in Aberdeenshire will form the 12th round of a 15-event calendar, as it joins the USA as new events on the schedule.

It is the first time the United Kingdom has hosted a round of the WRC since 2019, and BBC Sport will provide extensive live coverage of the rally.

It will also be a home round for new World Rally champion Elfyn Evans, who won the title in dramatic circumstances in Sardinia on Sunday after rival Oliver Solberg crashed at the end of the final stage.

In doing so, Evans became the first WRC champion from the UK in 25 years and joined the late Colin McRae and Richard Burns as the sport's top-level title winners.

Northern Ireland drivers Josh McErlean and Jon Armstrong also competed at the top level of the sport in 2026 and will be aiming to return next year.

In addition to Rally Scotland, the BBC's coverage will include five live stages plus the Power Stage on all WRC rounds, highlights programmes, plus digital clips and content across BBC platforms.

How Evans defied history to join rallying greats

Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC champion

The season will start on the icy tarmac roads in Monte Carlo from 21-24 January before rounds in the snow in Sweden and vast landscapes of Safari Rally Kenya.

Three tarmac events in a row then take place in Croatia, the Canary Islands and Japan, before the Acropolis Rally in Greece.

The WRC's Italian round moves from September to July, and will move from the gravel roads of Sardinia to tarmac in Rome.

The high-speed events in Estonia and Finland retain their back-to-back summer slots before the USA hosts its first WRC round in 39 years from 26-29 August.

The WRC last held a points-paying round in the USA at the Olympus Rally in 1988, and the championship will return as a gravel round after a successful candidate event in June.

Rally Scotland takes place in early October before a South American double-header, in Paraguay and Chile, and Rally Saudi Arabia round out the calendar.

The event in Saudi Arabia was set to end the 2026 season but it was cancelled due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Rally de Portugal will not feature in the 2027 calendar but is in talks to return in 2028.

The upcoming season will mark a new era of the sport with the introduction of a new promoter along with WRC27 regulations which will limit costs and reduce the horsepower of the top cars.

It will also mark the return of Ford as a manufacturer to the sport in a collaboration with the M-Sport banner.

2027 World Rally Championship calendar

Rallye Monte-Carlo 21-24 January

Acropolis Rally Greece 24-27 June

Rally Scotland 30 September-3 October

Rally del Paraguay 21-24 October

Rally Saudi Arabia 25-28 November

title: Gilmore says he expected difficult Quins start
description: Harlequins head coach Jason Gilmore says he expected a difficult start to the season following a summer of changes.
fullText:
Harlequins head coach Jason Gilmore says he expected a difficult start to the season following a summer of changes.

Quins are bottom of the Prem table after losing their first two matches.

They produced a woeful performance in Saturday's 48-0 thrashing by Gloucester - the club's heaviest league defeat for 26 years.

"We're certainly not going to be at our best early doors, but it won't be too far away," Gilmore told BBC Radio London.

"There will be bumps here and there, but the weekend wasn't one we can accept. We've just got to stick to task."

Having been in interim charge for six months after Danny Wilson left Harlequins to join Wales' coaching team, Gilmore was confirmed as permanent boss in March.

That was despite a miserable season in which Quins ended the campaign ninth in the table - their lowest finish for eight years.

Robbie Deans was brought in as performance director and there were further changes, with Rob Hunter, formerly of Exeter Chiefs, coming in as forwards coach and Brad Cooper arriving as attack coach.

Gloucester thrash sorry Quins to go top of the Prem

Quins display one of worst I have ever seen - Monye

Gilmore declared last month he had "no doubt" his side would perform better this time around, after a "new start" for the club.

But their performances so far suggest there is plenty of work to do.

He described the debacle against Gloucester as "unacceptable", but says a bumpy start was always likely.

"We've been learning a brand new attack system and we've got a brand new line-out system that we're putting in place that's going to take four to six weeks just to bed down," he added.

"We've got the international players that have just come back into the building as well that are learning it on the run.

"They've done their prep work, but there are two massive pieces of your game that we're still building and still learning."

Former Harlequins and England winger Ugo Monye called the abject display against Gloucester "one of the worst performances" he has ever seen.

"They got smashed in the scrum and line-out, their backfield coverage was poor, they got smashed at the gain line," Monye said on the Rugby Union Weekly podcast.

"They didn't score a single point in a league where they're literally handing out points for free."

And Gilmore has made his feelings clear to his squad.

He explained: "It's not 'going at' the players, it's more just being honest about things that we wanted to do that we didn't do.

"What we don't want to do is jump at shadows. We've had a pretty reasonable four weeks leading into that, so we've just got to get back on the tools and work as hard as we can and put out a good performance this weekend."

This Sunday, Harlequins are away to Sale, who claimed their first win of the season by beating Saracens last weekend despite having Jacques Vermeulen sent off.

"That's the beauty of sport - now you get your chance to redeem yourself," said Gilmore.

"If we could have played the game a bit sooner after the Gloucester game to get back out there, you'd definitely choose that.

"We're working hard this week in our prep, as the boys always do, and we're keen to go up there and show the best versions of ourselves."

title: Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?
description: The Court of Arbitration for Sport is set to rule on the decision to strip Senegal of their Afcon 2025 title. But fans should not expect an immediate verdict.
fullText:
Everyone knows a football match should take 90 minutes but, in its own way, the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) has been playing out for nearly nine months.

Now, finally, one team or the other - either Morocco or Senegal - willl grab the winner. Only that moment of glory will come in a courtroom, not on the pitch.

On Thursday, Sport's highest legal authority - the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) - will hear Senegal's appeal against the decision to strip them of the title they thought they had won back in January against the hosts in Rabat.

But those hungry for a resolution have already been warned it will not arrive on the same day.

So how did we get here? And what happens next?

In front of 66,000 home fans creating an electric atmosphere inside Rabat's Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Morocco appeared set for a date with destiny as they chased their first Afcon title since 1976.

Instead, the final descended into chaos deep into stoppage time.

With the match still goalless, Senegal thought Ismaila Sarr had scored a dramatic winner, only to discover that referee Jean Jacques Ndala had already blown for a Moroccan free-kick.

The controversy deepened in the 98th minute when, after a VAR review, Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty.

Tempers boiled over on the touchline and in the stands. Senegal coach Pape Thiaw led some of his players and staff down the tunnel, while supporters clashed with security as order briefly collapsed.

Play eventually resumed and, in the 124th minute, Morocco missed a golden chance to end their 50-year wait for continental glory when Real Madrid's Brahim Diaz failed to convert a penalty, chipping it 'Panenka' style into the grateful arms of goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Pape Gueye's extra-time strike then secured a 1-0 win for Senegal, who lifted the trophy for a second time.

'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Senegal's triumph

Senegal decries imprisonment of fans after Afcon clashes

Unsurprisingly the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FMRF) quickly lodged a complaint with the Confederation of African Football (Caf), arguing Senegal had breached competition regulations.

Article 82, contained within a chapter titled "Withdrawals", states: "If, for any reason whatsoever, a team… leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" they shall be "considered the loser and shall be eliminated from the current competition".

In March, a Caf appeals board agreed, ruling that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory.

While there is precedent for Caf overturning results during Afcon and World Cup qualifying, others, including one former senior Caf official, argued that only the referee has the authority to abandon a match if a walk-off occurs.

The FMRF said it was seeking the proper application of tournament regulations, but Senegal's federation (FSF) described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and appealed to Cas.

Afcon final 'deficiencies' dealt with - Motsepe

Denounce 'abject' Afcon decision - senior Caf member

Founded in 1984 and based in the Swiss city of Lausanne, Cas was set up as an independent legal body designed to settle disputes as global sport became more lucrative and, as a result, more litigious.

For governing bodies which recognise Cas' authority, it is deemed to be the supreme arbiter, meaning its ruling is final unless, in rare cases, Switzerland's highest court decides to set it aside based on a limited number of technicalities.

More than 900 cases are filed every year, from more than 50 different sports, covering issues such as employment contracts and transfers, doping, corruption, TV rights and, in this case, the organisation of sporting events.

The appeal will be heard by a panel of three arbitrators chosen by Cas for their expertise in sports law.

In this instance, the panel will be led by 76-year-old Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

If the panel fails to come to a consensus, its president will make the final decision.

How does Cas work and why can't Man City appeal to it?

While the hearing, which will be heard in private at the request of the parties involved, is expected to end on Thursday afternoon, Cas have already warned that this is merely the starting point of the panel's deliberation.

In a statement, the court warned it "cannot state when a final decision will be rendered but it will not be on the day of the hearing".

Having already waited nearly nine months to get to this stage, the bad news is that the Cas code states that appeal verdicts should be delivered a maximum of four months after a hearing, though guidelines also say panels should aim for less than three months.

The good news is that it can be quicker.

In 2020, Manchester City appealed to Cas over Uefa's decision to ban them from European club competitions for breaching financial fair play regulations.

The hearing took place on 8 June with the verdict landing in City's favour on 13 July.

Even though Caf's appeals board is independent, a reversal of its judgement would deliver another blow to the reputation of African football's governing body, which has already been heavily criticised for the retrospective decision to hand Morocco the title.

Caf president Patrice Motsepe said back in March that they will "adhere to" and "respect" whatever Cas decides, so if things go in Senegal's favour, it could mean someone having to tinker with the Afcon rulebook.

The Teranga Lions' walk-off has, however, already brought about a change in football's rules.

"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at ⁠a ​referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, back in April.

"This new rule will also apply ​to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match ​to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."

Thiaw has already been given his marching orders by Senegal, having lost his job following the team's last-32 World Cup exit, while Walid Regragui, the man in the Moroccan dugout back in January, was dismissed in March.

Both men will no doubt still view success with Cas as a moral victory.

Whatever the outcome, animosity is likely to linger between the two federations.

The FMRF's senior hierarchy were furious with Senegal's behaviour, believing the pictures beamed around the world irrevocably tarnished the image of the first Afcon hosted by the kingdom since 1988 - a tournament into which a huge amount of time and money had been invested.

The FSF and the Senegalese government have, meanwhile, leaned into a feeling prevalent across the continent that Morocco holds too much influence within African football.

Other incidents also irked them, such as laser pens being directed into players' eyes and ball boys moving goalkeeper Mendy's towel, something which eventually led to the barely believable sight of reserve keeper Yehvann Diouf being tackled to the ground by three ball boys when he tried to intervene.

With the next Afcon scheduled to take place in June and July next year, the chances of a high-profile rematch between Africa's best two teams is a tantalising thought.

But while the chaos of this year's final may have given birth to a new rivalry for fans to revel in, there is unanimous agreement that such encounters should be settled on the pitch and not in a courtroom.

Postponement not an option as Kenya races to be ready for Afcon 2027

title: How early-season data signals Scottish Premiership style shift
description: Underlying numbers from the start of the Scottish Premiership season suggest a refreshed approach could be taking hold across the league.
fullText:
Think of the Scottish Premiership and you think of a division with enough box-office drama and passion to rival, if not surpass, any other European league.

Where Scotland's top flight has had its perceived shortcomings over the years, though, is in the product and standard it offers on the pitch.

More blood and thunder. Less technical and tactical.

However, with more Premiership sides than ever showing a willingness to keep the high balls low, early-season data suggests the league is shifting towards a style many fans would regard as more attractive.

As domestic action resumes this weekend after an extended international break, the dust has been blown off the BBC Scotland supercomputer to uncover some underlying trends, with the help of stats gurus at Opta.

Are SPFL away ticket prices too expensive? And is price cap on agenda?

O'Neill 'just as determined' to lead Celtic

New boss Reedijk promises 'brave and intense' Hibs

There had long been a notion within Scottish football that it wasn't possible for most clubs to enjoy success on the pitch while entertaining their supporters with a progressive style.

Not got the technical ability of Virgil van Dijk or Kristoffer Ajer? Forget splitting your centre-backs either side of the six-yard box to collect a goal-kick and start an attack.

You don't have Callum McGregor in midfield? Best not ask your number six to drop deep and progress play under pressure.

It was all seen as too risky. Budgets wouldn't allow for it. Leave that to the big boys. That was the type of reasoning you would tend to hear.

However, those arguments were booted out of the park - or, more aptly, passed off the pitch - by Motherwell and Falkirk last season.

Scottish Premiership gameweek seven

Saturday, 10 October - Sunday, 11 October

Listen to coverage on BBC Sounds, watch highlights on BBC iPlayer, and follow live text updates on the BBC Sport website and app.

Jens Berthel Askou and John McGlynn demonstrated that exhilarating, free-flowing football could be played on a modest budget while still achieving success.

Both sides finished in the top half - Motherwell fourth and Falkirk sixth - and benefited from attendances spiking and a cash injection through transfer income in the summer, particularly at Fir Park.

That said, Derek McInnes' Hearts didn't receive too many plaudits for their playing style but were minutes away from one of the greatest triumphs in the history of the Scottish game.

That perhaps shines a light on a problem that can arise with these types of discussions. Snobbery can sometimes take over. At the end of the day, attractive football is what you deem to be attractive.

No Jambo would have cared about average possession or progressive passes had their team held out in May's dramatic title decider at Celtic Park.

Regardless, the success stories at Motherwell and Falkirk have clearly had an influence.

Dundee United boss Jim Goodwin was humble enough to reveal that Askou - now head coach at Toulouse in Ligue 1 - has inspired him to change his ways after more than 15 years as a player and manager in Scotland.

Goodwin's side are one of a number of Premiership teams to have undergone a stylistic shift this term, and that is reflected in the league's overall numbers, albeit the sample size remains small after just seven matches for each club.

Compared with the previous five Scottish top-flight seasons, passes per game have soared to 886. That is an increase of 58 on last term. Five years ago, the average was 795.

Passing accuracy is also at a high of 81%, which is quite a remarkable increase on the 73% recorded in 2023-24.

That is down to more short passing. The percentage of long passes across the league (13%) is now at its lowest level of the past five years. Perhaps surprisingly, Hearts and Rangers go long more than any other teams.

Goodwin's United, meanwhile, have gone from average possession of 42% last term to 50% this season. Their accurate passes per match have rocketed from 219 to 320.

It is a similar story for St Mirren under Craig McLeish and with Neil McCann's Kilmarnock, while league leaders Celtic and Alfred Johansson's Motherwell are locked at the top of the possession chart on 61%.

The promotion of St Johnstone back into the league, replacing Livingston, has added another side who aim to play a more expansive brand.

The recent appointment of Dutch head coach Marink Reedijk at Hibernian will only enhance that.

There is a counter view that the modern possession-based approach can lead to a stale watch.

A lot of fans would rather the ball was accelerated up to their forward players as quickly as possible, as opposed to their goalkeeper and centre-backs racking up their touch count.

However, although the goals-per-game average is currently at its lowest (2.5) since 2021-22, Premiership fans are seeing more shots per match (29) than in any of the past five campaigns.

But where are those efforts being taken from?

Strikes, and therefore goals, from outside the box are threatening to drop to a new low this term, mirroring a pattern across the sport in recent years as coaches continue to stress the need to create high-quality chances rather than take speculative shots.

That is another gripe of supporters who lament the thought of individualism being ripped out of the game. How many Bert Konterman thunderbolts or Shunsuke Nakamura screamers would now be lost with the trend to look for passes?

Yet many fans are just happy to see a refreshed approach, as they watch players they once thought only capable of hooking aimless balls and challenging for duels instead punch passes through the lines.

The Scottish game might be playing catch-up, but early 2026-27 data is potentially pointing towards unrivalled passion in the stands being reflected by a new wave of exciting football on the pitch.

title: 'Nothing impossible' as NI begin long road to Brazil
description: Northern Ireland defenders Nat Johnson and Rebecca Holloway tell BBC Sport NI of their dream of reaching a first ever Women's World Cup as NI go through the play-offs.
fullText:
A World Cup staged in Brazil is the stuff of dreams for any footballer and the chance to experience that is on offer for Northern Ireland as they begin their play-off journey against Portugal with hope of securing a spot at next year's tournament.

It will be a difficult ask for Michael McArdle's side, which has been hit by a spate of injuries and features five new faces, but there is a quiet confidence in the group before what will be, for some of them, the biggest games in their careers to date.

First up, in what is set to be an arduous journey in search of a World Cup debut, is Friday's home leg at Inver Park (19:30 BST) against the Portuguese.

"When you're growing up, Brazil is the place to be, it's the home of football. It really doesn't get much better than that," said Norwich City defender Natalie Johnson.

"The fact that we are at this point and that it could be a reality, you don't need much more motivation than that.

"There's a lot on the line, but we are taking it one game at a time and I think if you look at it that way, nothing is impossible. Obviously there is that dream at the end of it, but we're focused on the game in front of us."

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

As one of the lowest-ranked European sides in the play-offs, it is a difficult route to next summer's tournament for Northern Ireland.

If they overcome Portugal they will then face Croatia or Iceland in the next round. If they make it through those games, they will likely have an inter-continental play-off to make it the whole way to Brazil.

Portugal inflicted two defeats on in NI in Euro 2025 qualifying and sit 28 places higher in the Fifa world rankings, but Johnson and her side are not daunted by the task in front of them and instead want to embrace it.

"We absolutely believe these games are winnable," she added.

"We have a lot of experience in this team and the young players coming in bring their own individual experience and they really add to the squad. It's a good balance and we are going in to get something out of this.

"Any Portugal side is going to be very technical and we're expecting a very fast-paced game. We're going to have to be at our best to face that, quick football, and that's what we're working towards.

"On paper it might look like there is a big gap between the teams, but at the end of the day, it is a game of football and I think particularly on our home pitch it will be a much more level playing field."

Birmingham City defender Rebecca Holloway is one of the few survivors from the squad that qualified for Euro 2022, NI's first major tournament.

There have been a lot of changes to the squad since, but Holloway is excited for the future rather than dwelling on past achievements.

"It feels like a long time ago in a way, especially when you look at how much the squad has changed, but I think that's also what is very exciting," she said.

"It's like a new generation coming through and I think it's also important that we have some experienced players here to help those new faces. We're excited to see what they can do and encourage them to play with confidence and freedom and do what they are good at.

"We're slowly closing the gap on Portugal and the so-called bigger nations. They had a narrow 2-1 win over us at home in 2024 after a 4-0 away defeat, I think that shows that we are getting closer."

McArdle's youthful side do not have far to look for inspiration as to how to punch above their weight.

After assembling in camp on Monday, the team watched Northern Ireland's men's side 0-0 draw with Georgia.

That stalemate ensured Michael O'Neill's side stayed top of their Nations League group after picking up eight points from four games without conceding a goal.

"It was brilliant watching them play with such youth and energy and the exciting football that they are playing.

"This younger generation play with no fear and I think that is what the men's senior team are doing.

"I am hoping the young players see that and we can adopt the same attitude. I think we were all watching thinking we can't wait to do this on Friday."

title: How can home nations reach Women's World Cup?
description: England, Wales, Northern Ireland, Scotland and the Republic of Ireland are among those hoping to qualify for next year's Women's World Cup. What awaits them in the play-offs?
fullText:
England must get through two rounds of home and away ties to qualify for the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

Sarina Wiegman's European champions will play Greece in Crete in round one of the play-offs, with the first leg on Friday, 9 October at 17:30 BST.

The second leg will be played at home, at King Power Stadium in Leicester, on Tuesday, 13 October at 19:30 BST.

Commentary for both England matches will be on BBC Radio 5 Live.

Should England beat Greece over two games, they will face the winners of Slovakia v Ukraine, with the away fixture played first.

The exact dates of the potential second-leg fixtures are to be confirmed, although they will take place between 26 November and 5 December 2026.

England head coach Wiegman named her initial squad last month, with Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly notable absentees.

When asked why they were left out, Wiegman said: "They have not been playing to their full potential.

"Of course, I still believe in these players. They are really good and have shown so much for us."

Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "That is also why I didn't pick them this time, because they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks.

"I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and, of course, they want to work on that."

All you need to know about 2027 Women's World Cup

Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are also involved in the play-offs as they chase World Cup places.

As with England, they are in action on Friday.

In round one, Wales face Albania at 17:00 BST - with coverage on BBC Two Wales from 16:45 BST.

Scotland play the Czech Republic at 18:00 BST, available to watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Alba.

Northern Ireland take on Portugal at 19:00 BST, available on BBC iPlayer.

The Republic of Ireland will play Kazakhstan at 12:00 BST.

Despite England securing five wins from their six qualifying matches, world champions Spain finished top of the Lionesses' group and secured the one automatic spot.

Wiegman said: "We knew what the play-offs would look like and, while we're pleased with the draw against Greece, the focus now is on making sure we're really well prepared.

"We want to dominate games and have a lot of the ball and that's something we will prepare for carefully."

England did not want to go through the play-offs but were given an unkind draw in the qualifying groups when they met world champions Spain.

However, Wiegman's side are in a strong position for the play-offs and will fancy their chances against Greece, who sit 55 places beneath them in the Fifa world rankings.

England also beat potential round two opponents Ukraine in both matches in the qualifying group stage, with an aggregate 9-1 score.

Northern Ireland face a tricky tie against a talented young squad from Portugal in round one. Portugal twice beat Northern Ireland in Euro 2025 qualifying.

Their task gets even harder if they make it through to round two, with potential opponents Iceland proving to be difficult to break down in their matches against England this year.

Scotland are hoping to reach just their second Women's World Cup finals, after a 2019 appearance. They failed to qualify in 2023 but have performed well this year, including drawing with Belgium, showing that they can compete with Europe's strongest teams.

They would need to produce their best in round two if they meet big-hitters Sweden, who have been semi-finalists in the past two Women's World Cups.

Wales have never beaten a top-20 ranked nation in a competitive fixture and are likely to need to do so to qualify.

There is optimism, though, as Rhian Wilkinson's side thrashed play-off opponents Albania 4-0 in their qualifying group.

Elsewhere, having performed superbly in qualifying, the Republic of Ireland have a tough play-off route with Belgium potentially waiting in round two.

First, Carla Ward's side will have to navigate a 3,100-mile trip to Kazakhstan, to tackle relatively unknown opposition.

title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
description: The skipper who led India to the historic 2025 World Cup win has stepped down from her role in all three formats.
fullText:
When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.

India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.

That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.

Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.

Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.

Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.

Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.

The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.

In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.

Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.

Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.

Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.

Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.

Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.

Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.

"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.

"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.

"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."

Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.

In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.

The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.

Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.

Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.

Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.

The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.

She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.

An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.

Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.

That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.

The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.

Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.

Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.

India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.

With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

title: Toone comes into England squad as Bronze withdraws
description: Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone receives a late England call-up for this month's World Cup play-off games against Greece.
fullText:
Ella Toone has received a late call into the England squad for this month's Women's World Cup play-off ties against Greece.

Manchester United midfielder Toone, and Arsenal winger Chloe Kelly, were omitted from the initial squad with manager Sarina Wiegman saying "they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks".

Toone has scored 24 goals in 69 senior England appearances, winning Euro 2022 and Euro 2025 as well as starting in England's 2023 World Cup final defeat by Spain.

Toone said after being left out of the squad: "It's been a really difficult week. It's not the news that any footballer wants."

Meanwhile, Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze has left the squad and will return to her club to manage a minor injury sustained in league action last weekend against West Ham.

The Lionesses arrived in Crete on Wednesday evening to prepare for Friday's first leg against Greece at the Pankritio Stadium in Heraklion.

The second leg takes place at Leicester City's King Power Stadium on Tuesday, 13 October.

The winners face either Slovakia or Ukraine on 26 November and 5 December in a two-legged play-off to decide which team progresses to next year's Women's World Cup, which is being held in Brazil from 24 June to 25 July.

title: 'Are you accusing me of receiving money?' - what Guardiola has said about charges
description: BBC Sport examines Pep Guardiola's comments about the Manchester City financial rule-breaking case during his time managing the club.
fullText:
"Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

Comforting words of solidarity from a long-standing leader can be a great source of strength and unity at a time of crisis.

And many Manchester City fans will have felt just that after former manager Pep Guardiola posted on social media last week in response to the club being found guilty of deliberate financial rule-breaking over nine years.

To some, Guardiola's intervention came as a surprise. After all, he is no longer in a managerial position having left City in the summer, and so was under no obligation to comment.

In the past, Guardiola - who joined City in 2016, most of the way through the 2009-18 period the charges relate to - had insisted guilty verdicts would change his relationship with the club.

He was outspoken on some matters during his time in Manchester, including Catalan independence and Israel's military offensive in Gaza.

But in some instances he sidestepped questions on human rights in the United Arab Emirates, whose government includes key members of City's hierarchy, and didn't broach the UAE's alleged role in the ongoing conflict in Sudan, which has accused it of being complicit in genocide. The UAE has strongly rejected the allegations.

City are, of course, appealing against the guilty verdicts, and Guardiola remains employed by owners City Football Group as a global ambassador.

Next week he is expected to attend City's Champions League tie against Paris St-Germain - the club's first home match since the guilty verdicts were announced.

But what did he say about the Premier League's case against the club over the years?

BBC Sport has taken a look at every significant comment Guardiola made on the subject during his time in charge at Etihad Stadium.

Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City

"Do you know the question you're asking me?

"Did I receive money for another situation, right now, today? Honestly, do you think I deserve to have this type of question, the day we won the treble... did I receive money? Are you accusing me of receiving money?

"I listen to my chairman and my CEO, and I trust them. They tell me we are fair and we absolutely follow the rules. I believe them."

Guardiola's first comments on allegations of financial rule-breaking by Manchester City were delivered furiously, at a media conference in the immediate aftermath of a 6-0 victory over Watford in the FA Cup final.

He had been asked by Sky News' Rob Harris whether he had ever received separate, undeclared payments from the club in addition to his contracted salary, after the Football Leaks website published hacked information suggesting former manager Roberto Mancini had been paid in such a way.

Guardiola appeared to take the questions as an attack on his personal integrity.

Mancini said last month: "It's not an issue that concerns me. It's nothing new because this matter has been discussed for the last four or five years.

"Manchester City has not been found guilty, and the alleged double contract is not my concern. It's their issue, not mine."

19 February 2020 - bullish over Uefa appeal

"We appeal. When someone believes they are right, they have to fight. The club has to fight and I trust the club 100% what they have done and they have explained to me.

"This situation is not finished and we will wait. But until it is resolved you have to play and play, and that is what is going to happen."

Guardiola was responding after Uefa found City guilty of breaking its Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules, and banned the club from European competition for two years.

He was bullish regarding the club's right to appeal.

14 July 2020 - Champions League suspension overturned

"We were damaged. The people say we cheated and were lying - and many times. The presumption of innocence wasn't there."

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) had lifted the Uefa suspension and cleared the club of the more serious charges, finding some were unproven or that in some cases too much time had passed since the alleged rule-breaking.

Guardiola suggested in response that the wider football world had simply assumed the club was guilty and fair treatment had been lacking.

7 May 2022 - trust in City hierarchy

"Why did I defend the club and the people? It's because I work with them.

"When they are accused of something, I ask them: 'Tell me about that.' They explain and I believe them.

"I said to them: 'If you lie to me, the day after I am not here. I will be out and I will not be your friend any more. I put my faith in you because I believe you 100% from day one and I defend the club because of that.'"

Guardiola made clear he had built a level of trust with those in the City hierarchy that meant he inherently believed them.

But he also insisted he would resign if the club were found guilty, and distance himself from anyone who had 'lied' to him.

Guardiola had, of course, left the club in the months before the guilty verdict was confirmed last week. But in response he reaffirmed his kinship with City and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.

Manchester City and the 115 Charges Explained

10 February 2023 - first response to 115 charges

"My first thought is that we are already being condemned. I am fully convinced we will be innocent.

"Personally, I am happy we are here. We have the chance to defend [ourselves]. I think we have good lawyers. I think the Premier League, supported by 19 teams, will have good lawyers too.

"Just in case we are not innocent we will accept what the judge in the Premier League decides, but what happens if in the same situation that Uefa happened we are innocent - what happens to restore or pay back our damage?"

In an extraordinarily tense media conference after the Premier League announced it was pursuing 115 charges against City, Guardiola again insisted the club were innocent and suggested confidence their legal team would secure a result in their favour.

The Spaniard again suggested the media and public were predetermining City's guilt without a fair hearing.

23 May 2023 - frustration with process

"We would love [the verdict] tomorrow - this afternoon better than tomorrow.

"What we won on the pitch, we don't have any doubts."

A few months into a process that would take just over three and a half years, Guardiola expressed exasperation with the amount of time the Premier League investigation was taking and the doubt being placed on his team's achievements by pundits, the media and fans.

24 November 2023 - staying to manage in League One

"You are questioning like we have been punished. And in the moment, we are innocent until guilt is proved.

"I know the people want it. I know, I feel it. I will wait. Wait and see it and after the sentence has been done we will come here and explain it.

"There is more chance [for me] to stay if we are in League One than if we were in the Champions League."

Guardiola made two key pledges here - a media conference in response to the verdict when it was eventually revealed, and to continue managing the club in the lower leagues if such a punishment was handed down.

His summer exit thwarted the latter, but he would repeat the media conference promise later.

23 August 2024 - final weeks before hearing

"I am happy that it starts soon and hopefully it will finish soon. We will accept [the verdict], like we have always done."

In the months before the legal hearing into the charges began, Guardiola again expressed a desire for haste.

13 September & 21 September 2024 - hearing begins

"I know what people are looking for. I know what they are expecting - I know it because I have read it for many years.

"Everyone is innocent until guilt is proven. It's like everyone doesn't expect us to be not just relegated, they want us to disappear off the face of the earth."

Guardiola again insisted the football world was against City from the outset, as the legal hearing into the case began.

7 February 2025 - anticipating a final verdict

"In one month, I think there will be a verdict and sentence."

Briefings at the time indicated a verdict was expected in early 2025. Guardiola was under the same impression, but in reality it was a long way off.

The independent commission panel expressed its frustration with the time taken when it eventually published its findings last week.

23 May 2026 - leaving Manchester City

"I trust them. I spoke with them and trust how they behave and how they did. What happened, happened.

"If you find me, yeah, but that will be difficult."

On leaving City, Guardiola underlined his belief in the club's innocence for a final time and his belief that individuals in the club's hierarchy were telling the truth.

In the final line, Guardiola again insisted he would give a media conference once the verdict was given - if journalists could find him.

No such media conference has been announced. The only subsequent comment Guardiola has made was last week's social media post.

The post featured photos of him holding trophies and posing with key City ownership figures including Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano - the men under pressure - but no players.

What the verdict means for his legacy is something football fans around the world will determine for themselves.

title: Wakefield top as all 14 Super League clubs stay for 2027
description: The 14 Super League clubs will remain in place for 2027 with Grand Final winners Wakefield Trinity topping the IMG ratings.
fullText:
All 14 Super League clubs will remain in the competition next season after the release of the yearly gradings, with Wakefield Trinity topping the ratings for the first time.

Following their Super League Grand Final success, Wakefield have come top of the ratings, based on criteria formulated by media giant IMG, with marks for five factors - fan experience, finance, stadium, community and on-field performance.

London Broncos have come 16th on the list, below fellow Championship side Barrow Raiders, despite a season in which they won the second tier's Grand Final, the 1895 Cup and were runaway champions in the regular-season standings.

The Broncos were overlooked 12 months ago when Bradford Bulls, York Knights and Toulouse Olympique joined the expanded 14-team competition.

But, with the backing of Australian businessman Grant Wechsel, former Brisbane Broncos star Darren Lockyer and a squad full of internationals, they do still harbour hopes of playing in Super League in 2027.

Australia's National Rugby League (NRL) is looking to invest in the competition, with talks at an advanced stage.

It is understood any completed deal would involve the Australian governing body insisting on Broncos featuring in the top flight next season.

London Broncos rout Doncaster to clinch treble

What are IMG gradings and how do they work?

Wakefield have matched 2025 champions Hull KR's record grading score of 17.85 from 12 months ago, to continue their rise on and off the field under Matt Ellis' ownership. In the same rankings last year they were eighth with a mark of 15.47, only just above the threshold for Category A status.

"Wakefield Trinity's rise to the top of the 2026 club grading rankings is a fascinating story for rugby league, and a strong example of how sustained progress on and off the field can be recognised through the grading framework," said RFL chief executive Ian Nolan.

"Their achievement sits alongside encouraging movement across the sport, from growing attendances and digital audiences to continued improvements in facilities and community delivery."

Leeds Rhinos remain second, although their score of 17.03 is slightly lower than they achieved in the 2025 rankings.

Warrington Wolves have jumped from sixth to third on the back of a much stronger season which culminated in reaching the Grand Final at Old Trafford, only to lose to Wakefield.

It is fourth place again for Wigan, who won both the Challenge Cup and the League Leaders' shield, just above Hull KR and Leigh Leopards. St Helens drop from third to seventh after a season in which they missed out on the play-offs for the first time in the Super League era.

Castleford Tigers complete the Category A clubs as they have risen from 11th in 2025 to eighth and move into the top-tier section despite finishing 13th in Super League.

Catalans Dragons and Hull FC are ninth and 10th, but both have fallen from an A to a B grade. Then come Bradford Bulls and Huddersfield Giants, with Toulouse Olympique and York Knights, occupying 13th and 14th, albeit with higher scores than last year.

However, only six of the 14 Super League clubs have scored higher than they did 12 months ago.

But there was a significant gap to the teams outside. York's score of 13.24 was comfortably higher than the next best, Barrow with 9.85, while London only achieved 9.77, which was down on their mark of 11.65 from last year.

Overall, 26 clubs were graded on this system,, external split into three categories, A, B and C.

title: F1 heat hazard declared for fourth time this season
description: The Singapore Grand Prix is declared a heat-hazard race, the second weekend in a row that the designation has been used in Formula 1.
fullText:
The Singapore Grand Prix has been declared a heat-hazard race, the second weekend in a row that the designation has been used in Formula 1 and the fourth time this year.

The definition allows teams to fit cooling devices to their cars that pump liquid through a vest worn by the driver to manage temperatures in the cockpit.

A heat hazard is an official status for an event where it is forecast that temperatures will exceed 31C at some point during the race. It was first introduced in 2025.

This year's race is also being held amid air-quality issues as a result of smog caused by fires in Indonesia. F1 is monitoring the situation, which also applied at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, but does not currently consider it a cause for major concern.

Singapore is close to the equator and has long been known as one of the most demanding for drivers - in 2024, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton were treated for heat exhaustion after the race.

Temperatures in the city are always in the 31-33C region across the race weekend, with high humidity and a chance of rain every day.

The race is held at night, but temperatures remain in the region of 30C even after dark.

A cooling kit is not mandatory, but any driver who chooses not to use it has to carry 5kg of ballast in their car to ensure he does not have a competitive advantage.

The system uses a cooling tank and pump, usually situated in the car's nose, that delivers a cooled liquid, such as glycol, through a system of pipes in a fireproof top worn under their overalls.

Some teams and drivers prefer not to use the system because of two key compromises.

It is difficult to keep the liquid cool enough for long enough so that it lasts for an entire grand prix - a problem exacerbated in Singapore because it is the longest race of the year.

And some drivers find the cooling top uncomfortable in the tight confines of the cockpit.

If the liquid cannot be kept cool, it reverts to car temperature, which is considerably higher than ambient. It is not unusual for temperatures in an F1 cockpit to rise above 40C.

Mercedes are one of the teams who have decided against running the system because they preferred to devote the resource that would have been involved in making it robust enough to last a race into car performance.

Governing body the FIA has granted teams an allowance under the cost cap of $50,000 (£38,000) if they can make a system that keeps the liquid cool for an entire grand prix, and a further $75,000 (£57,000) if they could make the top comfortable.

Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord described the allowance as "small", adding: "We didn't believe that allowance was sufficient for us to be able to develop a solution that would be robust enough to last for the entire race."

Singapore follows the Austrian, Italian and last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia in being declared a heat-hazard race this year.

The Austrian and Italian races were held amid the Europe-wide heatwave that led to record temperatures across the continent.

The temperatures in Malaysia and Singapore are comparable with typical temperatures in south-east Asia. Had the heat-hazard designation existed before 2025, they would have fallen into that category numerous times in the past.

title: England to host 2031 Netball World Cup
description: England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031, when the sport's pinnacle event is held at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.
fullText:
England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031.

The quadrennial tournament will be held at Manchester's Co-op Live indoor arena, World Netball and England Netball announced on Thursday.

Liverpool staged the event when England last hosted in 2019.

World Netball president Liz Nicholl said: "After reviewing their strong bid, I am confident England Netball will host another thrilling international event, and I am excited to see what we can achieve together in 2031 and beyond."

Eastbourne put on the inaugural tournament in 1963, with Birmingham staging the 1995 edition.

England reached a World Cup final for the first time in 2023, but the Roses were denied a first title by 12-time winners Australia in Cape Town.

England also finished as runners-up in 1975, when the tournament was contested in a league format.

Baroness Sue Campbell, chair of England Netball, said: "To have the best netball players in the world coming to Manchester is a hugely exciting prospect, and I know the city will give them the welcome they deserve.

"This is a fantastic opportunity not only to showcase our sport on the biggest stage, but also to inspire the next generation of players and fans."

England Netball chief executive Fran Connolly said the tournament would provide "a powerful platform to grow the visibility, profile and impact of women's sport and netball across the UK".

The announcement comes in England Netball's centenary year.

The Co-op Live arena hosted this year's Netball Super League Grand Final between AO Thunder and London Pulse, which was played in front of more than 8,000 fans.

title: Clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal
description: Premier League clubs are "concerned" about political interference in Manchester City's appeal after Prime Minister Andy Burnham's comments.
fullText:
Some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by comments made by Andy Burnham - appearing to downplay the verdict against Manchester City - that they are now "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process, sources have told BBC Sport.

Senior club figures say they were shocked when they heard the prime minister tell the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club were found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

They have questioned what his comments to the BBC were designed to achieve, and said it had put the Independent Football Regulator in a difficult position.

Burnham is under increasing pressure surrounding his relationship with the club's Abu Dhabi ownership during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester.

Such is the level of scrutiny that Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

Despite clarification from Downing Street that Burnham's view is that no-one is "above the rules", his comments have sparked unease among some senior Labour figures who fear his initial comments have had major cut-through with voters.

Guardiola set to attend Man City v PSG next week

Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League

Your Manchester City Questions Answered By The Experts

Senior club sources have said they found the comments "absolutely bizarre", and that it was "at best naive and at worst quite manipulative, and that is not a good look".

A different source said it was "clumsy", while another said they were surprised that the prime minister had "misspoken".

The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League.

An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with a sanctions hearing still to come.

A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.

However, when asked about potential interference in the process off the back of Burnham's comments, one senior club source said: "Everyone would have a degree of concern. How much would depend on how much you read into that comment.

"I think everyone is concerned. Because no-one is stupid around the table. We understand the geopolitics as well. We understand the investment they have made in our country. I don't think anyone could doubt that or criticise that. But this is different, this is sport, this is our national game."

Another club source, however, said the degree of scrutiny on Burnham now means they think any interference would be impossible.

This is a sensitive area for the prime minister. Manchester City's dominance of English football has overlapped in large part both with a period of economic growth for the city of Manchester, and with Burnham's nine years as mayor from 2017 until earlier this year.

As mayor, Burnham championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester's economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city's leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

Regardless of Burnham's past career, there are additional sensitivities which would be true under other prime ministers too.

The UK as a whole is eager to trade with the UAE, and the country is an important diplomatic ally in the region at a time of turmoil and war.

When the guilty verdicts were announced, Richard Masters, the Premier League's chief executive, said the club had "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade".

Burnham's comments came in an interview with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason the next day.

When asked about 'Brand Manchester' taking a hit, the Prime Minister drew a parallel with a previous Premier League case with Everton, saying he still held the view "firmly" that they "weren't fairly treated".

Everton were deducted 10 points, later reduced to six on appeal, by an independent commission for breaching Premier League financial rules.

Asked if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city," he added.

Burnham's comments provoked strong criticism.

The following day, a No 10 spokesperson sought to clarify the comments, saying: "As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

However, this statement was amended following further criticism over the use of the word "if" - which was changed to "wherever".

The Premier League is viewed by governments of different political stripes as one of the country's major cultural exports, so ministers are eager for the row not to cause lasting damage to its brand.

Additionally, being a football fan is a core part of Burnham's political persona.

He is an Everton season ticket holder and, prior to becoming prime minister, he spoke of hoping to continue sitting in his usual seat at Hill Dickinson Stadium - but this has not been possible because of security concerns, as was the case for Sir Keir Starmer, his Arsenal-supporting predecessor.

Last month Burnham floated the prospect of lifting the ban on football fans drinking in the stands, though it was quickly clarified that this is not in fact government policy.

title: Snakes and jungle mind games as Bottas cycles to Singapore GP
description: Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas says he was chased by dogs, saw snakes and leapt over a lizard as he cycled from Malaysia to Singapore for this weekend's Grand Prix.
fullText:
Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas says he was chased by a dog, saw snakes and leapt over a lizard as he cycled from Malaysia to Singapore for this weekend's Grand Prix.

The Finnish driver arrived in Singapore on Wednesday after choosing a 260-mile (419km) bike ride over a flight from last weekend's Formula 1 race in Sepang, outside the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur.

The 37-year-old began his journey just hours after spinning out of Sunday's chaotic Grand Prix, taking a trip that involved off-road and gravel trails as well as cycling at night.

"I saw some snakes, which I was a little bit worried about, but actually they were pretty chill. They were just doing their thing," said Bottas.

"I saw one cobra, one python just crossing the path in front of me. I saw some of those big lizards that you also see here, one was on the path.

"I had to jump over it on a bike because I saw it last minute. I got chased by one dog, I got stuck behind a group of cows on one small track."

Bottas is an accomplished cyclist and earned a spot at the Gravel World Championships after finishing fifth in his age group at a qualifying event in the Czech Republic during Formula 1's summer hiatus.

Unfortunately for Bottas the World Championships take place this weekend as well, so he will be competing on four wheels instead of two.

When the Emilia Romagna Grand Prix was cancelled in 2023, Bottas decided to use the time to compete in a gravel race in Scotland.

Bottas has endured a difficult return to Formula 1 with new team Cadillac this season. He is 22nd in the drivers' standings, is yet to score a point after 16 Grands Prix and has failed to finish eight races.

"The wildest part was the riding at night in the jungle. The noise in there, your mind starts to play games," added Bottas.

"'What is out there? Who knows what is out there?' But then you just need to crack on and keep going."

title: Faster than F1: The extreme motorsport where women keep winning
description: Top Fuel drag racing is the only elite motorsport class where women frequently beat men to major titles.
fullText:
Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.

She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.

Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.

The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.

It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.

Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.

Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.

So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?

More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.

Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.

It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.

Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.

The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."

Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.

"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."

And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".

Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.

Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.

Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.

Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.

Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".

In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".

The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.

She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.

When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.

"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.

This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.

More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.

Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.

Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.

The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning

Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title

Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.

Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.

For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.

Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.

The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.

"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.

Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.

Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.

Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.

She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.

Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.

More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.

It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.

In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.

The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.

The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.

Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.

In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.

Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".

Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".

She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe
