title: How Brighton attract and develop the best young players ahead of their rivals
description: Brighton sporting director Mike Cave discusses Brighton's transfer policy and how the club signs and nurtures the best young talent in the game.
fullText:
Brighton & Hove Albion sit third in the Premier League, with one of the highest-scoring teams in Europe.

To the uninitiated it might seem logical that the Seagulls must have spent big, investing in players ready for the first team.

Yet Brighton are, along with Everton, one of only two clubs to record a profit in transfer spending over the past five years.

It is a team full of young players, testament to the club's data-led recruitment and development strategy.

"We have a really clear philosophy around how we can be competitive in arguably the most challenging league in the world," Brighton sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Sport.

But Brighton are more than just competitive. They went into the international break with a 3-0 home win over champions Arsenal.

From identifying players, to providing pathways, integrating them into the team and then selling at the right time, it is a strategy which has worked, year after year.

This is how the the club identify, attract and grow talent - and make them into first-team players.

Brighton use analytics and data as their primary method of tracking and identifying players.

Through club owner Tony Bloom's Jamestown Analytics, the performance of pretty much any player - or coach - who is in a professional league can be monitored.

"It helps us to identify talent from around the world in quite an efficient way," Cave said. "That allows us then to move quite quickly in what is a really competitive transfer market."

Just how Brighton's analytics set works is a closely guarded secret. But it does involve assessing a number of characteristics to identify signings who fit the club's model.

"There's no single attribute or a single metric that we particularly go after," Cave explained. "It's more trying to assess a player's performance and potential.

"It'd be great to break it down into one or two things but we're dealing with human beings playing a really complex game - sometimes in different parts of the world, in different leagues."

Over time, there is a constant re-evaluation. Success and failure help to refine how the data is interpreted.

The Seagulls, along with Brentford and more recently Bournemouth, are widely considered to be the best operators in this sector.

Many clubs have tried to copy it without achieving the same level of success.

But it is not about data alone.

"What's as important is the information we try to gather around the player's character, their background and their suitability for our environment," added Cave, who has been at Brighton since 2022 and was promoted to sporting director in the summer.

"Not every player would be right for Brighton and Brighton won't be right for every player either.

"We invest a good amount of time in trying to understand the individual, the person, the human being. Ultimately, this is a people industry.

"That's where the subjective and the non-football data really plays a huge part in our decision-making processes."

The Brighton Blueprint: How to Compete with Football's Giants

The use of the loan market, both domestically and in Europe, is crucial for the planned career development of many of Brighton's signings.

Since 2018-19, the Seagulls have agreed well over 20 loan deals in each campaign, with 27 last season. This summer, Brighton loaned out 16 players. More will follow in January.

"We've had over a period of time now a really productive and successful loan pathway," Cave explained.

"So we might identify players that we think have good potential, but maybe aren't quite ready for the Premier League.

"We believe we can offer one of the best developmental pathways, be it through the loans strategy that we have, or through our own under-21s programme."

Take Alexis Mac Allister, who was signed by Brighton for £6.8m in January 2019 but immediately loaned back to former club Argentinos Juniors, and then to Boca Juniors for 2019-20.

Only in the summer of 2020 did Mac Allister become a first-team player at the Amex.

The Argentina international, who won the World Cup in 2022, went on to make 112 appearances for the Seagulls before being sold to Liverpool for £35m. It would likely have been a higher transfer fee if the player's contract did not have a release clause.

Most recently, there is Jan Paul van Hecke. The defender was signed from NAC Breda for £6m as a 20-year-old in 2020, and spent two seasons on loan with Heerenveen and Blackburn Rovers.

The Netherlands international then became a first-team player and, after 131 matches for the Seagulls, was sold to Tottenham for £52m in the summer.

The fruits of the policy this season can be seen this season, with two players signed in the summer of 2024.

Malick Yalcouye, a £6m signing from Gothenburg, spent the past two years out on loan, first with Sturm Graz in Austria and then with Swansea City in the Championship.

The 20-year-old has two Premier League goals in his first five appearances.

Ibrahim Osman, a £17m capture from Danish side Nordsjaelland, was with Feyenoord in the Netherlands, Auxerre in France and Championship side Birmingham City.

The 21-year-old winger has made three substitute appearances so far.

"Malik's had a really good start to the season," Cave said. "Osman is another young player who has had three loans now and then has come back into the squad for this season.

"They're good examples and role models of a commitment to their own development, having an attitude and a desire to want to get better.

"Now we're starting to see them delivering in the Premier League for us which is a fantastic success story but real testament to them and their hard work."

One to watch this season is Matias Orozco, an 18-year-old who cost £3.75m from Deportivo Calli. He is with Castellon, who sit second in the Spanish second division.

The defensive midfielder was handed his first senior caps for Colombia during the current international break.

"We do a lot of work in analysing the right clubs, coaches, leagues, understanding how complex it is, to find the right destination," Cave added.

"Depending on where that player is in their career, what areas of their game we're looking to help develop, or as just part of their maturity and experience."

Brighton have shown - from Mac Allister to Carlos Baleba, who was sold to Manchester United in the summer - that they can be a stepping stone for an ambitious player. And that reputation is crucial in a competitive market.

"The key thing is being able to demonstrate to young players that we have a plan," Cave said.

"Depending on the age, that can be over one year, or several years. Hopefully, that leads to playing in our senior team.

"That track record of being able to nurture young talent in different ways plays a big part in why a number of players agree to come to Brighton."

For Cave, "arguably the most critical part" is integrating players into the city and the culture of English life.

"We can have all the data, all the character backgrounds, context and information that's available," Cave added.

"But ultimately when that individual and their family arrives in Brighton, how we onboard them, how we embed them, how we make them feel like it's their home all contributes to them being the best version of themselves on the football pitch.

"We want players to come to Brighton and thrive and enjoy the city, enjoy the football club."

Brighton have a reputation as one of the most savvy operators, but they are also one of the most prolific.

Over the past five seasons, the Seagulls have made 62 permanent signings. Only Chelsea, on 72, have made more of clubs to be in the Premier League throughout.

"It offers the opportunity to recruit a wider base of talent and that's probably why you've seen the scale of our recruitment over a period of time," Cave said.

"We try to have a longer-term view on how we can build the squad over a period of time."

There is one stark difference between the two clubs. Brighton recorded a transfer profit of £10m, while Chelsea show a deficit of £721m.

Though player trading is clearly important when it comes to the financial regulations, Cave insists the club do not "ever set out thinking about how we're going to sell a player".

"Ultimately, we recruit them to come and perform and develop for Brighton," Cave added.

"Like nearly every club in in the world, at some point players choose to leave or depart a football club. That's just a natural cycle."

Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella, Mac Allister and Joao Pedro were all sold for a profit in excess of £25m each. In Caicedo's case, it was £77.5m.

"The important thing is to maximise the sale of that player, because that goes back into the football club to reinvest, to hopefully, again, improve the squad," Cave added.

Alongside the emergence of Yalcouye and Osman has been the rise of Charalampos Kostoulas, who was signed from Olympiakos for £30m in the summer of 2025, just after his 18th birthday.

When Danny Welbeck was sold to Chelsea the loss of his goals - he scored 13 in the Premier League last season - could have been a concern.

Kostoulas was bedded in last season and now has four goals from six starts across all competitions this term.

Luka Vuskovic, the 19-year-old club record transfer from Spurs, has seamlessly replaced Van Hecke.

Chema Andres, 21, looks to be another astute summer purchase in midfield after Baleba's departure.

Signed from Stuttgart for £18m, Andres is a Spain Under-21 international who came through the Real Madrid academy. His one season in the German Bundesliga feels like the kind of loan Brighton would have done had they signed him directly.

Three hugely promising young players signed to replace key stars.

"It's fundamentally around having had a consistent strategy over a period of time that we can then try to improve," Cave said.

"Over a period of time now we've had real faith and confidence in the potential of young players to come into the league and perform at the highest level"

They knocked Manchester United out of the EFL Cup, coming from two goals down to win 3-2.

Next week, Brighton begin their Conference League campaign at home to Lithuanian outfit FK Kauno Zalgiris.

The club are the clear favourites to win the competition, which would be the first major trophy in the club's 125-year history.

The club does not really need vindication of their vision and long-term plan, but some silverware would be nice.

title: Engine size limits and working with Iraola - the Liverpool academy approach
description: Liverpool academy director Alex Inglethorpe talks to BBC Sport about the value and future of Liverpool's academy.
fullText:
One of the first things you notice in Alex Inglethorpe's office at Liverpool's AXA Training Centre is a framed image gifted by Trent Alexander-Arnold.

It is a picture from 2019 of the academy director and player watching a game together. Alexander-Arnold left for a new challenge at Real Madrid last year, after 20 years on Merseyside, but his story is one of inspiration for everyone that enters Liverpool's academy.

He joined as a six-year-old in 2004 and went on to win the Premier League, Champions League, FA Cup, League Cup, Community Shield, Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Club World Cup with Liverpool.

"The ideal for any academy, and certainly for us, is wanting young players - and hopefully they're local players - to improve the first team and in doing so, they come and win trophies," says Inglethorpe.

"At Liverpool the bar is high, so to have a player capable of winning everything that you could possibly win is a dream."

Inglethorpe and his team oversee the development of younger players and ensure there is alignment between the academy and the first team.

One of the phrases used is 'the first team pitch is only 300 metres away from the academy building in Kirkby, but the journey might take 10 years to get there'.

Under new boss Andoni Iraola, players like Rio Ngumoha, Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and James McConnell, who have spent time at the academy, have all featured this season.

"We were fortunate because of how the calendar worked, with players still at the World Cup and a delayed return. Andoni and his staff spent a lot of his first week here watching the academy," says Inglethorpe.

"So we felt ahead, in terms of building a relationship from the outset."

At the Kirkby academy, phones are handed in on a morning and there is a clause in contracts with a maximum engine size limit for cars that are driven into academy premises.

"It comes back to passing your audition. First impressions matter," says Inglethorpe.

"Often before you've kicked a ball, the car you drive or the watch you wear can have an impact on how you're thought of - and that could be first team staff or players looking at you.

"We've believed in the idea of 'earning the right' for some time."

Last week, Manchester United signed 16-year-old winger Isaac Konde from Liverpool on a one-year scholarship followed by a five-year professional deal. Both clubs are now in talks over a compensation package.

In February, a tribunal ruled Liverpool must pay at least £2.8m to Chelsea for Ngumoha. The 18-year-old left Chelsea in September 2024 to join the Reds and signed his first professional contract a year later.

Both are recent examples of the current climate around talent.

At Liverpool, the belief is they have been sensible and responsible with a view to deferred gratification in most cases, but the wage structure is currently under review.

"It's always a compliment when other clubs want your players as it means you're doing something right," says Inglethorpe.

"But I think the market of players at 16 is distorted because of Brexit and because you can't recruit like you would do before. There's always been movement of players but it feels a little more extreme now.

"When there's a clamour for talent - fees, wages and everything else will shift accordingly, so it's dealing with what we have and adapting to a new situation."

When Curtis Jones moved to Inter Milan in the summer, it left Liverpool without a first team player born in the city.

"I acknowledge the fact that ideally Liverpool would love to have a team full of Scousers," says Inglethorpe.

"But it is testament to the supporters that if you adopt the characteristics of a Scouser - and you only have to see the likes of Bill Shankly, Kenny Dalglish and others over the years - you can be treated as one of their own.

"So if you are fearless, passionate, play tough and demonstrate those qualities, then it doesn't matter if you've come from an L1 postcode and got a purple bin or not. That's the beauty of the club and the crowd."

One name to keep an eye on is 15-year-old Luca Eden. The midfielder was born in the Wirral and has already represented England at youth level.

Last month, he became the youngest player to feature in the Uefa Youth League for Liverpool, beating a record previously held by Joshua Abe, Ngumoha and Alexander-Arnold.

"We've got plenty of Scousers in the academy and plenty who I think will play for the club. But if not and a lad comes from Warrington or wherever, that's not a problem," Inglethorpe insists.

One of the most challenging aspects of Inglethorpe's role is letting players go. Liverpool released eight players from their academy set-up at the end of last season.

Inglethorpe explains how the likes of Harry Kane, who was coming through the academy at Spurs when he was a youth coach there, and Alexander-Arnold weren't necessarily the best in their respective youth cohorts.

"At that stage, there's too many unknowns. You can't predict how players will react to adversity and natural bumps in the road," says Inglethorpe.

"I've been proven wrong so many times in the past. A good example would be Jarell [Quansah] - someone who was always liked and never in danger of leaving but probably never seen in the top three in the group."

Quansah left Liverpool for Bayer Leverkusen in 2025 and has since won eight caps for England.

"There are no certainties - the point of the academy is to allow them to fulfil their potential," says Inglethorpe.

"Sometimes players need to leave to gain an opportunity. There are lots of lovely examples of boys leaving and having good careers, and I'm not convinced they would have had the same career if they stayed at Liverpool.

"The linear and most productive way is to break in, but there's different pathways that can lead back to playing for Liverpool - and that is the dream."

Just before the academy players go on the pitch, there is a sign that says: "Don't look sideways" - referring to where the first team train.

Next month will mark 14 years at Liverpool for Inglethorpe. So what's his definition of success?

"Anyone would want to take something on and leave it in a better place, and I think we've done that," he says. "Ultimately we have had players in the first team winning major trophies and we're fortunate to be part of that era."

The 'Kids Cup', when Liverpool beat Chelsea in the 2024 Carabao Cup final. Faced with an injury crisis, Jurgen Klopp relied heavily on academy players and his side finished the match with a team whose average age was under 22. Klopp called it his "most special trophy".

"It's definitely a moment in time. The longer the game went on, Jurgen was taking off the seniors and putting another one of the boys on. It was an incredible show of belief," says Inglethorpe.

On another wall in Inglethorpe's office is a magnetic board with headshots of every player in the academy on the left and the first team squad on the right. Ultimately, the motive is for everyone to make the journey across the board.

With a £20m revamp to the academy facility planned to be completed by 2028, the determination to carry on producing first team players is stronger than ever.

"There are exciting times ahead with the potential for the other end, and I'm really excited for the future," says Inglethorpe.

"In Julian Ward [the new sporting director], we have someone who is hugely invested in the academy and has been on this journey for a long time."

title: Ronald Acuña Jr. fights back tears after the Braves' Division Series elimination by the Dodgers
description: cut his postgame media scrum short at his locker as his eyes welled up with tears.The former MVP and five-time All-Star was overcome with emotion as he tried to explain his role in the Atlanta Braves' exit from the NL Division Series with Thursday night's 4-1 loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 4.
fullText:
ATLANTA (AP) — Ronald Acuña Jr. cut his postgame media scrum short at his locker as his eyes welled up with tears.

The former MVP and five-time All-Star was overcome with emotion as he tried to explain his role in the Atlanta Braves' exit from the NL Division Series with Thursday night's 4-1 loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 4.

"I feel like I did nothing to help the team this series," Acuña said through Braves interpreter Franco Garcia. "You know, I'm supposed to be a spark plug for my team out there, and I never lit that fire. And so, extremely disappointed."

Acuña said his sore knee, on which he had an MRI after Game 3 to check for a potential injury, was not a factor in his performance.

Acuña was 2 for 15 in the series with no home runs and no RBIs. There was a smattering of boos at Truist Park after he grounded out in his final at-bat to finish the night 0 for 3.

"It's frustrating just because I know the talent that I have," he said before he sat down and cut off questions.

There was more to the Braves' offensive struggles than just Acuña. Matt Olson and Drake Baldwin, Atlanta's other two top hitters, were just as unproductive. The trio went a combined 5 for 45 (.111) with no homers and one RBI against a Dodgers pitching staff that looks capable of leading the franchise to its third straight World Series title. The three sluggers were 0 for 11 in the clincher.

As a team, the Braves hit .145 in the series and averaged two runs per game, a quiet end to a season in which they won 94 games and the NL East title under first-year manager Walt Weiss.

"Losing is definitely the number one (frustration)," said Baldwin, whose eyes were also red from tears. "(Winning is) the only goal, but just not coming through. I mean, most of it relates back to that. It's doing what we can to win games and execute that."

Due to a combination of injuries and scheduling, the Braves were forced to use two bullpen games to start the series at Dodger Stadium, and Atlanta managed to get a split. But with the Braves' top two starting pitchers available at home, the offense dried up. Atlanta scored just two runs in two games.

"The Dodgers have something to do with that," Weiss said. "They're going for their third straight world championship for a reason. Their arms just keep coming at you.

"But that's the postseason. You never know what you're going to get. It's very unpredictable. But some guys, you have a lot of unsung heroes a lot of times in the postseason, and sometimes guys struggle. It's obviously magnified because you're playing under a microscope. We struggled with runners in scoring position. So did the Dodgers. The games were really tight."

Austin Riley, who hit a three-run homer to send the Braves to a victory over the Phillies in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, also struggled against the Dodgers' star-studded rotation of Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Tyler Glasnow.

Should the Braves' offense be given a little grace, given who they were facing?

"The competitive side of me is like, no, but you know, they're tough," Riley said. "They're a tough group, they really are. But at the same time, in order to get to where we want to be, we've got to be able put together hits and score runs against those guys."

title: Liberty on brink despite Stewart's record-setting Game 2 performance
description: New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart imposed her will against the Atlanta Dream in Game 2, scoring 25 of her 35 points in the first half.
fullText:
Playoff Stewie is fully activated.

New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart imposed her will on Game 2 of the WNBA playoff semifinal series against the Atlanta Dream on Wednesday, Oct. 7, becoming the first player in WNBA playoff history to record 35 points, 10-plus rebounds and five-plus assists. Stewart finished with 11 boards and six assists.

However, Stewart's monster stat line wasn't enough to get New York over the finish line. The Liberty lost 101-98 in overtime to drop into an 2-0 hole against the Dream as the best-of-five semifinal series shifts to New York for Game 3.

The Liberty failed to use their remaining reset timeout with 4.3 seconds remaining in overtime while trailing 101-98. New York advanced the ball up the court and Stewart got off a game-tying 3-point attempt to no avail.

Stewart expressed frustration over the Liberty's unused reset timeout, saying she specifically asked the referees if they had one during Dream forward Angele Reese's free throw attempts with 4.3 seconds remaining. Stewart said she was told the Liberty had no reset timeouts, despite having one.

"I asked Kevin (Fahy), I said, 'Do we have a reset timeout?' And he said, 'I'm going to check at the table,'" Stewart recalled. "So then he looked to Fatou (Cissoko-Stephens) and she said, 'No.' So then he told me no. Of course, who knows what would happen in the game, but we would have hopefully a better shot on goal."

The Liberty were looking for Stewart early and often on Wednesday. She had 15 points in the first quarter, shooting 5-of-6 from the field and 2-of-2 from the 3-point line. She added another 10 points in the second quarter to improve to 8-of-9 from the field, 2-of-2 from the 3-point line and 7-of-9 from the free-throw line.

Stewart became the first player in league history to record 25 points in a half while shooting at least 80% from the field.

"(Breanna Stewart) hit some big shots early and just continues to find ways to attack in the paint and at the free-throw line," said Liberty guard Sabrina Ionescu, who finished with 10 points and six assists.

Stewart's 25-point first half is tied for the third-highest scoring half in playoff history. Angel McCoughtry holds the record with 27 points scored in a half in 2012, while Stewart recorded 26 points in a half in 2022.

However, Stewart's production slowed in the second half as the Dream's stout defense zeroed in. She was limited to eight points in the second half, shooting 2-of-8 from the field across the last two quarters. Stewart added two points in overtime.

She finished with 35 points, 11 rebounds, six assists, two blocks and one steal, shooting 11-of-20 from the field and 2-of-4 from the 3-point line and 11-of-13 from the free throw line. Wednesday marked the 10th 30-point playoff game of Stewart's career, but Stewart would rather have the win as the Liberty are on the brink of elimination.

"We're focused on winning one game and that's (Game 3 on) Friday. And then we go from there," Stewart added. "But this group has experience. I've been a part of some crazy series and I have a lot of confidence in our group... that when we get home... play in front of our fans and put it all out there."

title: Dodgers survive Atlanta. Their greatness - and flaws - will be for all to see in NLCS
description: Dodgers fought off Atlanta to rach the NLCS. But the team has some major questions to answer.
fullText:
The on-field celebration was so brief you could have missed it, as appropriate for Game 62 in Phoenix as a clinching Game 4 of the National League Division Series. The clubhouse histrionics were soggy, the words from Miguel Rojas and Dave Roberts poignant as ever, befitting a journey that's now reached 166 games. Yet the booze fountain slowed after a 10-minute burst.

When you win your eighth consecutive postseason series, are aiming for your third consecutive World Series championship, all part of 14 consecutive trips to the playoffs, there's a certain mastery in toeing the fine line between "act like you've been there" and appreciating just how very hard it is.

The Dodgers know. And this particular romp through October is about to get much more difficult.

The Atlanta Braves made the Dodgers aware of their own mortality for about 36 hours of this National League Division Series. And then a Braves team that was outmanned in the best of times but significantly diminished after surviving a wild card series folded in the face of all that deluxe Dodgers depth.

This NLDS ended Wednesday, Oct. 7, when the Dodgers pushed across three runs in the final three innings to register a 4-1 victory and eliminate Atlanta in four games.

It was workmanlike, "grindy," as they like to say, in some ways an ideal level of rigor to begin this playoff run. Yet the Braves' ample resistance was, due to their three-game survival of their wild-card series against Philadelphia, compromised.

To steal a metaphor from Atlanta's exurban ballpark, the Dodgers Beat the Freeze. But in the National League Championship Series and, perhaps, World Series to come, they'll no longer have a head start.

"We understand that the job's not done. We have eight more wins. Stay focused," Roberts told his team. "There's no more talented team than the Los Angeles Dodgers. We're smarter, we're better and we're tougher."

Probably all true. Yet it's fair to wonder if "better" applies when it matters most – right now.

The Dodgers won 100 games, yet a bevy of injuries and ailments that dogged them in the latter portion of the season seemed evident against Atlanta.

Will Smith, their backbone of a catcher who received all 73 innings of their seven-game World Series triumph in 2025 and never really seemed to recover, went 1-for-16.

Blake Snell, dogged by shoulder and groin woes all season, did not get out of the fourth inning of his Game 2 start. Tyler Glasnow was good for four innings in Game 4.

And of course, Shohei Ohtani was nowhere to be seen on the mound – and virtually invisible in the batter's box.

The two-way superstar reduced to an ailing DH had two singles in 15 at-bats, struck out four times and had Roberts searching for hope before Game 4, noting his at-bats were better, and that his "misses are better because they are to the big part of the field versus hitting the ball on the ground, to the right side of the infield."

Well, in his final at-bat of the NLDS, Ohtani hit the ball on the ground, to the right side of the infield, just 85 mph off the bat against a fading Tyler Mahle in the seventh inning.

An hour later, the champagne flying, Roberts told Fox Sports in a clubhouse interview: "If we're going to win eight more games, we're going to need Shohei."

Of course, these are the Dodgers, and the sky will be blue tomorrow. Max Muncy and Kiké Hernandez are forever, the former slamming three home runs and the latter playing the joker role perfectly against Chris Sale, crushing his 17th career postseason homer off the 6-6 ace.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto is on a historic run, ever the unicorn in this postseason of openers and four-and-poor starters. And relievers Edwín Diaz and Tanner Scott, signed for $69 million and $72 million the past two seasons, are both healthy and locking down the eighth and ninth innings, with Edgardo Henriquez's heat a nice middle-inning bridge.

Playing a seven-inning game against this collection of talent is daunting. But the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays and New York Yankees are complete teams, blessed with either real postseason rotations or a force of nature like Jacob Misiorowski.

They're the type of teams that expose opponents' weaknesses, that will make Teoscar Hernández's left field adventures prove far more penal, that will grind the Snells and Glasnows into early showers, and, in the case of the Brewers, have come back to October baseball again and again and again.

One of these times, they will break through. One of these times, the Dodgers won't survive that moment that, a few weeks later, might cause them to wonder, "How did we pull that off?"

Or maybe they will. Appropriately, this Dodgers run is shaping up a little bit like the 2000 Yankees. The last team to threepeat survived an 87-win campaign to win their division, survived plucky Oakland and potent Seattle to reach a World Series where they steamrolled the Mets.

Eventually, all that Yankee experience mattered.

These Dodgers know their gravitas matters, too. And heck, they won 100 games, easily winning their division, and seven innings of Yamamoto.

So come Wednesday night, they celebrated again, not too hard but also soaking up every drop. A core that took nearly a decade to win its first World Series knows how fragile all this is.

Fortunately, they ran into a Braves team ready to crack. Now, the true tests await, the Dodgers' greatness – and deficiencies – about ready to go under the microscope.

title: Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh's struggling unit gets called out
description: For years, Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh’s exceptional track record allowed him to largely escape blame, even when the Sooners struggled to score. He's getting plenty of criticism heading into Saturday's game against Texas in Dallas
fullText:
Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh's struggling unit gets called out originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

NORMAN, Okla. -- For years, Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh's exceptional track record allowed him to largely escape blame, even when the Sooners struggled to score.

He earned that pass with a lengthy run of success. He has coached 14 NFL draft picks since joining the staff in 2013, including NFL stars Orlando Brown and Creed Humphrey. He was a finalist for the Broyles Award as the nation's top assistant coach in 2017 and a semifinalist in 2018. His lines have blocked for Heisman-winning quarterbacks Baker Mayfield and Kyler Murray.

Times have changed. Bedenbaugh is getting plenty of heat heading into Saturday's game against Texas in Dallas amidst a stretch of three games during which the Sooners have scored a combined 37 points, failed to break 300 yards and lost twice.

Even the media is acting differently. Generally, when there have been questions about the offense, reporters have focused on skill players. Now, Bedenbaugh's offensive line is a primary target, along with offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle.

Venables didn't protect Bedenbaugh or the unit when asked about the offensive line on Tuesday.

"It's been incredibly inconsistent, very disappointing," Venables said.

Here's Brent Venables today being brutally honest about the state of Oklahoma's offensive line: "It's been incredibly inconsistent and very disappointing. As you build your football team, that's a critical place. That is a place that probably requires the most development of any position that you have on your roster." "Very uneven job when it comes to choosing the guys that we've brought in here. Way too many guys are coming and going at that position group...It's been very unstable and certainly not the kind of development that you want from top to bottom." #Sooners:

Venables said one factor in the offensive line's struggles is that players switch schools so often that it is hard to develop players, which negates one of Bedenbaugh's greatest strengths. He also said because so many players bounce around, building continuity is difficult.

"That is a place that probably requires the most development at any position that you have on your roster and we haven't allowed, for lots of different reasons … the portal's the No. 1 reason," Venables said.

Venables said it's not all on Bedenbaugh. He hinted that some of the offensive linemen missing games are "injured players" who should be on the field.

"Some guys -- that guy's always hurt," Venables said. "And so if you look at, just peel it back on our roster, you can figure out who maybe that's been."

Peeling it back, left tackle Michael Fasusi has missed three games and most of the other with a shoulder injury, center Jake Maikkula has missed one game (knee) and right guard Ryan Fodje (knee) has missed one game. Fasusi was listed as doubtful for the Texas game on Wednesday's SEC injury report and left guard Eddy Pierre-Louis is listed as questionable with an undisclosed injury.

Venables, perhaps realizing what he implied, tried to be a bit more understanding as he continued.

"Some of it's dumb luck," he said. "Everybody goes to the same practice, they're in through the same drills. Some guys get hurt, some guys don't. It's football. It's a physical, violent game, and we've had some bad luck there."

MORE:Oklahoma offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle is unpopular with Sooners fans

Venables said the future looks bright if the Sooners can keep their young talent. Fasusi and Fodje are sophomores. Fasusi started 10 games as a freshman and Fodje started six games as a freshman.

"It's going to be incredibly important to bring back a good majority of the guys that are already here, that are young guys, that are developing as we speak, but it's been very unstable and certainly not the kind of development that you want from top to bottom," he said.

title: Fan interference denies Anthony Volpe a tying homer for Yankees against Rays in Game 3 of ALDS
description: Volpe was denied a game-tying homer in ALDS Game 3 after umpires ruled fan interference on his deep drive to left field.
fullText:
NEW YORK — Anthony Volpe was denied a tying home run for the New York Yankees in Game 3 of their AL Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays when umpires ruled a fan interfered with his drive to deep left field Wednesday night.

The play was initially called a two-run homer that would have tied the score at 4 with two outs in the sixth inning. But a lengthy video review by Major League Baseball determined a fan reached over the wall to catch the ball as Rays left fielder Victor Mesa Jr. tried in vain for a leaping grab.

Spectator interference became the ruling, and Volpe was awarded an RBI double that scored George Lombard Jr. from first base, trimming Tampa Bay's lead to 4-3 at Yankee Stadium.

There was another slight delay after some fans in left threw debris onto the field, and Spencer Jones then struck out against Griffin Jax to end the inning.

"After viewing all relevant angles, the Replay Official definitively determined the spectator interfered with the ball over the field of play. The ball would not have left the playing field nor would it have been caught. The call is OVERTURNED, there was spectator interference and no home run. Additionally, the Replay Official scored one run and placed the batter-runner at 2B," MLB said in a statement from the Replay Center.

Mesa hit a tiebreaking, two-run homer off Max Fried in the top of the sixth to put Tampa Bay ahead.

The AL East champion Rays came in leading the best-of-five series 2-0.

title: Cubs BCB After Dark: Should fielders need to stay in their spots?
description: The late-night/early-morning spot for Cubs fans asks if more restrictions on fielding is needed.
fullText:
It's the end of another week here at BCB After Dark: the grooviest after-party for night owls, early risers, new parents and Cubs fans abroad. Come on in and sit with us for a while. There's no cover charge. The dress code is casual. There are a few tables available, or sit with someone new. Bring your own beverage.

BCB After Dark is the place for you to talk baseball, music, movies, or anything else you need to get off your chest, as long as it is within the rules of the site. The late-nighters are encouraged to get the party started, but everyone else is invited to join in as you wake up the next morning and into the afternoon.

Last night I asked you whether or not the Cubs should try to trade Matt Shaw and/or Pedro Ramírez. With the obvious caveat that we can't know what either of these two players would bring back in a deal, 57 percent of would try to trade Matt Shaw. Another 26 percent would just keep both players. Only 12 percent would trade Ramírez.

Here's the part with the music and the movies. You're welcome to join us there. Or not. We don't want you to do anything that makes you uncomfortable.

I saw a bunch of Christmas stuff for sale in a department store today, so I guess I have to start with the Halloween music before it's too late.

So let's kick the season off with Ella Fitzgerald singing "Old Devil Moon" from Finian's Rainbow, written by Burton Lane and Yip Harburg.

This is a live performance from 1969.

Despite my admitted squeamishness, I promised you that I would try to push my boundaries a bit and watch some horror films this month. I wasn't going to wade into the Saw series or anything, but I did vow to go a bit out of my comfort zone. After all, last year I got through Suspiria (1977). I can probably handle something stronger than the Universal Monster movies.

So far, I'm not pushing any boundaries. This week I watched The Cars That Ate Paris (1974) for one reason: it's the debut feature film by accomplished Australian New Wave director Peter Weir. Weir would go on to direct several classic films, earning him four Academy Award nominations (no wins), including one of my favorite films of the 1990s, The Truman Show. Which, if you come to think about it, is a bit of a horror movie itself, even if there is no graphic violence in it.

But The Cars That Ate Paris has 

The Paris of this film isn't the big one in France, but rather a small town somewhere in the Australian countryside. Woe be it to anyone who drives through Paris, because there are traps set up to cause car crashes, as well as warring gangs that drive around in tricked-out cars that are supposed to look like monsters. This town in the middle of nowhere survives by salvaging the wrecks of the cars, as well as taking the survivors to a hospital where they are subjected to horrific medical experiments and organ harvesting.

Terry Camilleri plays Arthur, a passenger in a car being driven by his brother who is unfortunate enough to drive through Paris. (Camilleri is best-known for a part he would play 15 years later, Napoleon in Bill and Ted's Excellent Adventure.) Arthur's brother is killed in the crash, but Arthur survives. The town's mayor (John Meillon) takes pity on Arthur and rather than send him to the hospital for experimentation, he adopts him into his own family. He's already done this with a few young women who became his "daughters," but now he's decided that he wants a son and Arthur is elected.

To be clear, Arthur has no choice in this matter. For one, the car gangs prevent anyone from leaving Paris whom they don't want to let leave. Secondly, Arthur had killed a pedestrian while driving years earlier. Although he was exonerated from manslaughter charges, Arthur now has an intense pathological fear of driving. So he can't drive out of town and there's zero public transportation in this tiny town of a few hundred people.

But unsurprisingly from what we know about the rest of his career, Weir isn't really interested much in the murderous car gangs or the grisly experiments in the hospital. The good middle hour of this 90 minute movie deals more with Arthur's psychic trauma and the mayor's war with the car gangs for control of the town. And while Weir and cinematographer John McLean make the whole thing look good, it's a long slog between the car crashes that start the films and the final 15 minutes when a war breaks out. And unfortunately, it's not a terribly interesting slog.

The gore is pretty limited to a few staged shots of the mangled victims of crashes. There is a kind of cool "hedgehog" car that is tricked out with wild spikes everywhere and yes, someone does get mangled on it. But the reveal of the "hedgehog" is held back until near the end of the film. The other "monster" cars that we see earlier just aren't as visually compelling.

The other issue is that one of the reasons The Wicker Man works is that while the audience knows the island is hiding a deep, dark secret, we don't know exactly what that secret is or what they are planning until the very end of the film. The Cars That Ate Paris goes down the same road of a small, isolated town with a dark secret, except that everyone is pretty open about what that secret is from the very beginning. Certainly the audience knows what's up pretty quickly. There just isn't much suspense going on here.

I did like the fake-out of the opening scene that made the movie look like it was going to be a cigarette or soft drink commercial until it ends in a bloody crash. The film was a bit downhill from there.

You can tell that The Cars That Ate Paris was made by a director with some talent. Even without the benefit of hindsight, there are just a lot of interesting shots that capture the desolate isolation of rural Australia. But it seems to me that Weir is fighting between the ridiculousness of the concept and his desire to make a more serious psychological drama, succeeding at neither.

To be clear, The Cars That Ate Paris isn't a bad film. The people involved are just too skilled and put in too much effort for that. But it is an unsuccessful film in that it doesn't really manage to grab the audience and when it tries, it's just not quite sure which direction it wants to take us in.

However, Stanley Kubrick loved The Cars That Ate Paris and began recommending Weir for film projects in the US on the basis of it, as well as Weir's second film, Picnic at Hanging Rock. So maybe I'm wrong.

Here's a trailer for The Cars That Ate Paris. You can certainly get a sense of how good the film looks from this. Maybe that Peter Weir has a future.

Welcome back to everyone who skips the music and movies.

It's no secret that MLB thinks fielding is too good. Or more specifically, they're upset that fielders are turning too many balls in play into outs and that is sending batting averages into free fall. Only seven players hit .300 or better in 2026. This year, the league average for batting average was .244. Back in 2006, the league average .269 and that's with pitchers hitting for half of the teams.

Baseball originally tried to fix this problem by preventing teams from putting three infielders on either side of second base. The shift had become ubiquitous in MLB in the 2010s and it was hoped that by banning it, batting averages would increase.

The plan didn't work because infielders are just too good these days. It didn't seem to make much of a difference if the shortstop was one step to the left of second base or two steps to the right. The infielders still got to most balls and turned most of them into outs.

Now MLB is experimenting with a new plan, as outlined by Eric Longenhagen in Fangraphs (Free to read). MLB has been very quiet about this as there has been no announcement that anyone was doing this, but Longenhagen noticed it while watching games in the Arizona Fall League.

You can read the article to see what MLB is trying. Basically, MLB is dictating where fielders must stand before a pitch is thrown. There are green hashmarks on the dirt and the outfield grass and an outfielder must be in that spot before the pitch is thrown. The hashmarks correspond with roughly where players traditionally stood, although it seems like the outfielders have to play fairly shallow. When there are men on base, infielders are allowed to move around as before but outfielders are still rooted to the green hashmark in the outfield.

The details of this are all a little fuzzy because MLB hasn't announced any of this publicly. Longenhagen suggests that MLB may also be experimenting on where to put the hashmarks and that they may be moved to different spots later in the AFL season. The rules also appear to be in effect only in games at Salt River Field, so we don't have a lot of data yet on what it means.

So what do you think of this proposal? Personally, I hate it. It seems like a gimmicky and artificial way to try to increase offense. It also appears to be another way that MLB tries to punish "smart" teams so that "dumb" (read: cheap small-market) teams can compete without spending money on an analytics department to determine where fielders should stand. It also seems like they're forcing outfielders to play unnaturally shallow in order to get more extra-base hits over their heads. (Although as Longenhagen notes, that may just be what they're testing over the first few weeks and maybe they'll move them farther back later in the season.)

I also love good defense and want to see it rewarded, although I'm not clear on whether this proposal does that or not. You can see how a fielder like Pete Crow-Armstrong might be able to make a lot more plays even standing in an unnatural position than a lot of other outfielders.

If you want contrary opinion, Brett Taylor over at Bleacher Nation "kinda" likes it. On the other hand, Craig Calcaterra hates it, saying that someone in MLB thinks this dumb idea was a good idea:

It's probably many of the same people who thought playing a game in the Grand Tetons was a good enough idea to approach the government with it.

I can link to the piece, but it's from Calcaterra's paid newsletter and if you subscribe, you've probably read it already.

So now it's your turn. What do you think of this radical limitations on fielder positioning?

Thanks for stopping by tonight and all week. It's good to stay together in the off-season. Please get home safely. Tell your friends about us. Leave us five stars. Recycle any cans and bottles. Tip your waitstaff. And join us again next week for more BCB After Dark.

title: OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websites
description: Exclusive: Revelation comes after company’s executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write...
fullText:
Exclusive: Revelation comes after company’s executive told parliamentary inquiry he did not believe AI had been used to write message

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.

On Tuesday, one of the company’s executives told a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believe that its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.

Guardian Australia understands AI was used by OpenAI’s legal and security teams to generate parts of the wording of the email, including word selection and formatting of the message. But a source with knowledge of the incident said humans reviewed the final email, and humans were responsible for actually sending the communication to the Services Australia inbox.

OpenAI was contacted for comment.

An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June. The company notified Australia on 10 September despite becoming aware of the incident in August.

The company’s first notification to Australia came in a five-paragraph email to a Services Australia inbox, publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au, which was only checked once per day.

OpenAI has come under fire for not raising the issue in a more formal or direct way, including during a face-to-face meeting between the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, and Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on 1 September, nine days before the company emailed Services Australia but nearly a month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.

Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, admitted in a parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that the company’s “response was not good enough, and we should have informed the impacted parties much sooner”.

During the hearing, Liberal MP Aaron Violi – the shadow minister for technology – had asked Kwon specifically about the email and whether AI had been involved in its creation.

“I appreciate that, to get the data and have a review, you’ve got to use AI agents, and obviously your business uses AI. When you notified Services Australia via email, did your staff use AI to construct that email?” Violi asked.

Kwon responded: “I don’t believe so, but we’re happy to go and confirm.”

Kwon indicated during the hearing that OpenAI would provide specific responses to more technical queries in answers to questions on notice.OpenAI is expected to provide more information about the email once its own investigation has concluded.

The email, obtained by Guardian Australia in September, advised Services Australia: “We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI model activity involving Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics service at medicarestatistics.humanservices.gov.au.

“An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password. It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server.”

The email advised that OpenAI’s review “found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access”, and sent information about the “affected URL” and “affected report”.

“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available.

Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science and technology, spoke about the OpenAI incident in a speech in Sydney on Thursday, describing the company’s agent as having “hacked into an Australian government system”.

“As a starting point, no company should release a frontier AI model that is not safe,” he said.

“Yet the fact that has occurred, and the fact that the labs did not detect or prevent it, prompts important questions about the role of new regulation in the National AI Standards.”

Charlton said frontier AI “pushes the limits” of existing government conventions and protocols around assessing safety risks, and went beyond “conventional” approaches.

The assistant minister said “the market will not fix” issues with AI development, a contrast to the United States’ approach of letting companies operate with a degree of self-regulation. Charlton raised concerns that “frontier labs are putting capability ahead of safety”, positing that Australia can have the most impact on the development of AI by hosting and influencing frontier labs.

“AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them, and sometimes invisible until they arrive,” he said.

“The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves.”

Texas executes man using same drug involved in Christa Pike's failed lethal injection
description:
— A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee’s failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike a week ago.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m.
fullText:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee's failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike a week ago.

Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was convicted of killing Vickie Swartout, 42, in a 2000 store robbery caught on surveillance video.

Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to some members of his victim's family, who watched through a window just feet from the death chamber.

"I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness," he said, shortly before the injection got underway. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

He also thanked his friends and family and said he loved them, adding he was "in a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y'all." He concluded with: "Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y'all."

As the pentobarbital began taking effect, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped. He then began making snoring sounds, coughed and resumed the snoring sounds, each time the sound becoming quieter. Within about 30 seconds, all movement stopped.

He was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.

His sister was among witnesses watching through a window from an adjacent room and became distraught, exclaiming several times: "Get me out of here." She was assisted by corrections officers in exiting the witness room.

Texas has executed seven people so far in 2026, including Howard, and plans two more executions later this year.

Howard's attorneys unsuccessfully sought to block the execution by arguing that he was intellectually disabled and that he faced risks similar to those in Pike's case because both states use pentobarbital for lethal injections.

Pike's lawyers continue to seek more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old woman survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. Her lawyers said she was unconscious at a hospital after the attempt but was awake and speaking by Tuesday.

Howard was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during the robbery. Evidence presented at trial included surveillance video showing Howard shooting Swartout.

Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in Silsbee, a small, rural town about 100 miles (160 kilometers) northeast of Houston, according to court records.

In bidding to halt Howard's execution, his attorneys had filed a motion hours earlier before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals raising concerns about the quality of Texas' execution drugs. The court denied that request and a second filing involving the drugs without comment.

His attorneys also argued unsuccessfully to the U.S. Supreme Court that Howard's execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people, though it gave states some discretion in determining such disabilities.

The state told the court that Howard's lawyers did not present evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.

The high court late Wednesday declined to intervene, without comment, clearing the way for the execution.

Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.

Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution that was scheduled to be carried out in his state this year.

Stengle reported from Fort Worth, Texas.

fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Democratic Party officials sued US President Donald Trump on Wednesday, seeking a court order blocking his administration from ‌using taxpayer money to pay for election-related TV ads.

The lawsuit, filed by ‌the Democratic National Committee in federal court in Washington, accused Trump of a "blatant violation of the statutory ​ban on the use of appropriations for 'publicity or propaganda purposes.'"

Taxpayer-funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking a bipartisan backlash.

In a post on his Truth Social site on Monday, Trump said he considered the ads to be "a positive promotion for ‌our Great U.S.A." but that ⁠they would no longer be funded by taxpayers. The White House said this week his MAGA PAC would fund the ads.

The ⁠DNC, the main governing organization of the Democratic Party, said in its lawsuit that the ads continued to air after Trump's comments.

"With less than 30 days remaining before the midterm ​election ​and millions of public dollars apportioned to pay ​for propaganda ads still unspent, ‌the DNC has no choice but to take action in defense of free and fair elections," the lawsuit stated.

The ads ran during football games as recently as Sunday and during other programming. The New York Times reported that Trump personally directed the White House budget director to use taxpayer money for the TV spots, citing sources.

One ‌ad features Trump declaring that "America will never be ​a communist country" while a chorus repeats the ​words "love me." Another combines images of ​Mount Rushmore with footage of Trump praising a "golden age of ‌America."

Another new ad recently has featured ousted ​Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. ​A source briefed on the matter told Reuters the government-funded ads will end this week.

The White House said Trump's political action committee will not reimburse ​taxpayers for the ads ‌that have run to date.

The ads end with a disclaimer saying they ​were paid for by the US government.

title: Michael Dell defends Trump Accounts' shift to individual company stocks
description:
Michael Dell, philanthropist and founder of Dell Technologies, pushed back against critics who argue that allowing wealthy investors to donate individual company stocks to Trump Accounts could have a nefarious impact.
Under new rules that took effect last week, charities can put individual stocks into kids' accounts as a donation. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment vehicles that can be used for education expenses, starting a business, or saving for retirement. They were authorized in last year's One Big Beautiful Tax bill. Previously, the money was required to be invested in low-cost index funds.
fullText:
Michael Dell, philanthropist and founder of Dell Technologies, pushed back against critics who argue that allowing wealthy investors to donate individual company stocks to Trump Accounts could have a nefarious impact.

Under new rules that took effect last week, charities can put individual stocks into kids' accounts as a donation. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment vehicles that can be used for education expenses, starting a business, or saving for retirement. They were authorized in last year's One Big Beautiful Tax bill. Previously, the money was required to be invested in low-cost index funds.

So far, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell is the only donor to announce a major stock contribution, pledging more than 2 million shares to benefit lower-income children ages 11 to 17 living in lower-income areas.

"It's kind of hard for me to believe that's a bad thing, right?" Dell said Wednesday in an interview with Yahoo Finance. "That these children are going to somehow be negatively influenced because they now have one share of SpaceX, but they didn't have before, right? The alternative is they didn't have it, right?"

He continued, "It seems unlikely that that is some kind of devious plot to somehow influence these 2 million children. If anything, they're going to be interested in space and capitalism and how capital markets work, compounding and investing, and it will spark an interest in them that hopefully helps them as they become adults."

Critics say the rule change could tie a child's long-term financial security to a single company rather than the broader economy, and they've raised ethical concerns that billionaire donors could use multibillion-dollar stock dumps into kids' portfolios to manipulate asset prices or secure tax write-offs.

Dell and his wife, Susan, have pledged to donate $6.25 billion to invest $250 in the Trump Accounts of 25 million children across America. More than 10 million children have now received the contribution, representing $2.6 billion invested. By Friday, the full $6.25 billion is expected to be invested.

"I believe there will be a number of additional philanthropists that join us," said Dell. "We have now many employers that are joining in the fund here and either matching the government's contribution or going much larger and contributing to the accounts of the children that work inside their companies or even children in the communities where they operate their businesses."
